what-is-mahjong.title: 麻雀とは？初心者のための完全ガイド
what-is-mahjong.description: 麻雀は四人で遊ぶ牌を使ったゲームで、技術・戦略・運が絡みます。麻雀とは何か、牌の構成、世界各地の主要ルール、そしてオンラインでよく見かける牌合わせゲームとの違いを解説します。

sections.heading: 麻雀は四人で遊ぶ牌ゲーム
body: 麻雀（麻将）は、技術・戦略・少しの運が絡み合う四人用の牌ゲームです。各プレイヤーは13枚の手牌から始め、順番に牌を引き、捨て、誰かが和了形（伝統的には四面子一雀頭）を完成させるまで続けます。
19世紀の中国で生まれ、アジアを経て世界に広がり、地域ごとに異なるルールが生まれました。今日では世界で最もプレイされているゲームの一つであり、このサイトのような場所では完全無料でオンライン対局できます。

sections.heading: 牌の構成
body: 標準的な麻雀セットは144枚の牌で構成されます。数牌三種、字牌（風牌と三元牌）、そして一部のルールで使われるボーナス牌（花牌と季牌）です。
数牌は萬子（万、ten）、索子（条、bamboo）、筒子（筒、circles）の三種で、それぞれ1から9まで、各牌4枚ずつあります。字牌は四風（東・南・西・北）と三元牌（中・發・白）です。

sections.heading: 目的
body: 目標は四面子一雀頭の手牌を完成させることです。面子は刻子（同じ牌3枚）か順子（同じスートの連続3枚）のいずれか。雀頭は同じ牌2枚の対子です。
ルールによっては、和了には最低限の点数（飜、翻、ポイントなどと呼ばれる）も必要です。これが麻雀に深みを与えます——形が揃っただけでは和了にならない場合があるのです。

sections.heading: 主なルールバリエーション
body: 麻雀の遊び方は地域によって大きく異なります：
• 中国麻雀（香港スタイル）：日本以外で最も一般的。最低3飜が必要。
• 日本リーチ麻雀：リーチ宣言、ドラ、厳格な点数計算を持つ競技向けルール。
• 中国公式（MCR）：国際大会ルール。最低8点が必要。
• アメリカ麻雀：ジョーカー、花牌、年次ハンドカードを使用。
• 台湾麻雀：13枚ではなく16枚でプレイ。
• 四川麻雀：字牌なし、和了後も続行する高速な「血戦」形式。

sections.heading: 麻雀ソリティア vs 四人麻雀
body: 欧米の多くのサイトでは、一人用の牌合わせパズルを「麻雀」と呼んでいます——これは実際には麻雀ソリティアという全く別のゲームです。ソリティアは重なった牌を同じ牌同士で消していくパズル。本物の麻雀は、引く・捨てる・鳴く・点数計算を伴う対戦ゲームです。
どちらも楽しく、どちらもここでは無料で遊べます。このガイドは四人麻雀について説明します。

sections.heading: 麻雀はギャンブル？
body: いいえ。麻雀は技術を要するゲームで、ポーカーやチェスと同様、楽しみのためにも、賭けのためにも遊べます。このサイトでは完全無料——賭け金も、課金通貨も、現金賞品もありません。

sections.heading: 始め方
body: 最も良い学び方は、実際に打つことです。香港麻雀の卓（最初に学ぶのに最も易しいルール）から始めるか、「麻雀の遊び方」でステップバイステップのガイドを読んでください。慣れてきたら、日本リーチや中国公式に挑戦して、より深い戦略を楽しみましょう。

faq.question: 麻雀セットには牌が何枚ありますか？
faq.answer: 標準セットは144枚：数牌108枚（三スート）、字牌28枚（風牌と三元牌）、ボーナス牌8枚（花牌と季牌）。一部のルールではボーナス牌を除きます。

faq.question: 麻雀は覚えるのが難しいですか？
faq.answer: 基本ルールはシンプル：1枚引き、1枚捨て、四面子一雀頭を作る。点数は少し時間がかかりますが、最低3飜の香港ルールは優しい入門点です。

faq.question: 麻雀にお金は必要ですか？
faq.answer: いいえ。麻雀は楽しみのために、お金なしでプレイできます。当サイトの卓は完全無料で、賭け金は一切ありません。

faq.question: 一人で麻雀はできますか？
faq.answer: 本物の麻雀には四人必要ですが、オンラインではいつでもコンピューター対戦相手とプレイできます。一人プレイが好きなら、麻雀ソリティアという別の一人用パズルがあります。

faq.question: 麻雀と麻雀ソリティアの違いは？
faq.answer: 麻雀は引く・捨てる・点数計算を伴う四人対戦ゲーム。麻雀ソリティアは重なった牌を同じ牌同士で消す一人用パズル。別ゲーム、同じ牌。

how-to-play-mahjong.title: 麻雀の遊び方：初心者向けステップガイド
how-to-play-mahjong.description: 麻雀をゼロから学ぶ：牌、壁の構築、引く・切る、ポン・チー・カン、そして和了までを分かりやすく解説。

sections.heading: 必要なもの
body: 四人のプレイヤーと144枚の牌セットが必要です。各プレイヤーは卓の一辺に座り、それを席（風）と呼びます。親（東）が局を開始します。
オンラインでは、コンピューターが配牌、山の管理、点数計算をすべて行うため、手牌作りに集中するだけで済みます。

sections.heading: 山を作り、配牌する
body: 牌は裏向きにシャッフルされ、各辺17段の二重の壁として積み上げられます。各プレイヤーが一辺分を構築します。
親がサイコロを振って壁を崩す位置を決め、各プレイヤーに13枚が配られます（親は14枚を持ち、最初に捨てます）。オンラインでは、これらはすべて自動で行われます。

sections.heading: 自分の番：引いて捨てる
body: 自分の番では、山から1枚引き、手牌を確認し、1枚を中央に表向きで捨てます。常に13枚の手牌を保ちます。
その過程で、手牌を四面子一雀頭に仕上げるのが目標です。

sections.heading: 鳴き：ポン・チー・カン
body: 他のプレイヤーが捨てた牌が必要な牌のとき、引く代わりに鳴くことができます：
• ポン（碰）：捨て牌を取って、同じ牌3枚の刻子を完成させる。
• チー（吃）：捨て牌を取って順子（連続3枚）を完成させる——ただし左隣のプレイヤーからのみ可能。
• カン（杠）：捨て牌を取って同じ牌4枚の槓子を完成させる。
鳴くと手牌が開く（晒す）ため、狙える役が減る場合があります——本当に役立つときだけ鳴きましょう。

sections.heading: 和了する
body: 和了形は四面子一雀頭です。ツモ（自摸）で和了するか、他のプレイヤーの捨て牌を取ってロン（栄和）することもできます。
多くのルールでは最低点数も必要です。香港スタイルは最低3飜、中国公式は8点、日本リーチは最低1役が必要です。当サイトの卓では、聴牌までの距離を表示し、各和了の点数内訳を説明します。

sections.heading: 点数の基本
body: 点数は手牌に組み込まれた役から得られます。よくある役には、清一色、対々和、三元牌や風牌の刻子、そして七対子などがあります。
ルールによって役の価値は異なります。最もシンプルな考え方は、手牌の構造が整うほど高得点になる、ということです。和了後の点数内訳で、どこから点数が付いたかを正確に確認できます。

sections.heading: 今すぐ試す
body: 最も早い学び方は、実際に打つことです。香港麻雀から始めましょう——三人のコンピューター対戦相手、任意の聴牌ヒント、毎局の完全な点数内訳付きです。

faq.question: 最初に何枚の牌を持ちますか？
faq.answer: 各プレイヤーは13枚から始めます。親は14枚を持ち最初に捨て、最初の捨て牌以降は全員13枚を保ちます。

faq.question: ポンとカンの違いは？
faq.answer: ポンは同じ牌3枚、カンは同じ牌4枚。カンは面子に加え、山の端から追加で1枚引きます。

faq.question: どのプレイヤーの捨て牌でも鳴けますか？
faq.answer: ポンやカンはどのプレイヤーの捨て牌からでも鳴けます。チー（順子）は左隣のプレイヤーからのみ鳴け、巡目順を公平に保ちます。

faq.question: 「聴牌」やテンパイとは？
faq.answer: 聴牌（テンパイ）は、あと1枚で完成する手牌の状態。聴牌中は、正しい牌が来た瞬間に和了できます。

faq.question: 和了に必要な点数は？
faq.answer: ルールによる：香港は3飜、日本リーチは最低1役、中国公式は8点。当サイトの卓は最低点数を表示し、点数内訳を示します。

how-to-win-mahjong.title: 麻雀で勝つ方法：初心者向け戦略
how-to-win-mahjong.description: 実践的な麻雀初心者戦略：早めに方向を決め、孤立した字牌を切り、捨て牌を読み、鳴きすぎず、より早く聴牌する。

sections.heading: 早めに方向を決める
body: 最初の数巡で手牌を見て、どんな形を目指すか決めましょう。一つのスートが7〜8枚ある手牌は清一色を狙えます。対子や刻子が多い手牌は対々和を狙えます。字牌が一切ない手牌は断幺九に近い状態です。
早めに方向を決めることで、牌を計画に沿って捨てられるようになります。これが勝ち組と負け組を分ける最大の違いです。

sections.heading: 孤立した字牌を先に捨てる
body: 風牌と三元牌は最も対子や刻子を作りにくい牌です。孤立した字牌は初心者の手牌にほとんど役立たないので、不利になる前に早めに捨てましょう。
例外：役立つ字牌（三元牌や自風など）の対子や刻子がある場合は残す——それは待っている得点役です。

sections.heading: 捨て牌（河）を読む
body: すべての捨て牌は情報です。三人が索子を捨てていれば、必要な索子はまだ安全な可能性が高い。全員が萬子を保持していれば、萬子は集められており入手が難しい。
捨て牌を見ることで、相手の和了を完成させる牌を捨てるのを避けることもできます。

sections.heading: 鳴きすぎない
body: 鳴くと手牌が開き、得点役が使えなくなります。多くのルールでは門前（晒していない）手牌の方が高得点です。
初心者向けのルール：鳴きで聴牌まであと1〜2枚になる場合だけ鳴く。それ以外は引き続け、手牌を門前のまま保ちましょう。

sections.heading: できるだけ早く聴牌する
body: 最初に聴牌したプレイヤーが通常勝ちます。使えない牌を使える可能性のある牌と交換し、手牌の形を柔軟に保ちましょう——複数の牌で和了できる手牌は、1枚だけ待つ手牌より強いです。
当サイトの卓には聴牌までの距離を示すヒントがあり、自分で距離を見極める練習になります。

sections.heading: よくある和了形を覚える
body: 以下の形は頻繁に現れるので、覚えておく価値があります：
• 断幺九：1・9・字牌なし。ほぼどんな手牌からも狙える。
• 清一色：一つのスートだけの牌。高得点。
• 対々和（碰碰胡）：すべての面子が刻子。
• 七対子：定番の代替和了形。
• 三元牌の刻子：多くのルールで得点になる。

sections.heading: 汎用ルールではなく、自分のルールで打つ
body: 香港、リーチ、中国公式では重視するものが異なります。香港は素早く安い3飜和了を評価します。リーチは門前で構造の整った手牌とリーチ自体を評価します。中国公式は本格的な8点の役を要求します。
一つのルールを選んでその役を学びましょう——早く切り替えすぎると、最も早く混乱する方法です。

faq.question: 最も早くテンパイに到達する方法は？
faq.answer: 手牌を柔軟に保ち、安く確実な役を狙う。断幺九は初心者に最も早い——ほぼどんな開始手牌からも作れます。

faq.question: 鳴くべき？門前を保つべき？
faq.answer: 初心者は、鳴きで聴牌まで行ける場合以外は門前を保ちましょう。開いた手牌は得点が低く、情報を与えます。

faq.question: 相手の和了牌を出すのを避けるには？
faq.answer: 捨て牌を見守る。終盤では、他のプレイヤーが集めていた牌——特に聴牌している相手の牌——を捨てないよう注意。

faq.question: 勝つのは運か技術か？
faq.answer: 一局には運が絡みますが、セッション全体では技術が支配的。手牌の方向、捨て牌の規律、役の知識が、最もよく勝つ人を決めます。

faq.question: 最も和了しやすいルールは？
faq.answer: 香港麻雀は最低点数が最も低く（3飜）、初心者に最も寛容。勝つ習慣を学ぶ最良の場所です。

mahjong-rules-beginners-complete-guide.title: 麻雀のルール完全ガイド：初心者向け
mahjong-rules-beginners-complete-guide.description: 初心者向けの麻雀ルール完全ガイド。牌、壁、引く・切る、鳴き、和了と計算を解説し、主要なルールをわかりやすく比較します。

sections.heading: 麻雀のルールを一段落で
body: 四人が144枚の牌で手牌を作ります。各巡、1枚引いて1枚捨て、四面子一雀頭を完成させます。面子は刻子か順子。手牌が完成し、ルールの最低点数を満たせば和了を宣言します。それがゲームの全体像——あとは詳細です。
このガイドでは、その段落のすべての要素を順を追って解説し、初めてのプレイヤーが座って打てるようにします。

sections.heading: 牌
body: 標準セットは144枚：数牌108枚、字牌28枚、ボーナス牌8枚。数牌は萬子（wàn）、索子（tiáo）、筒子（tóng）の三種で、1から9まで各4枚。
字牌は四風（東・南・西・北）と三元牌（中・發・白）。花牌と季牌は一部のルールで登場し、通常は面子を作るのではなく小さなボーナスを与えます。

sections.heading: 山と配牌
body: すべての牌を裏向きにシャッフルし、各プレイヤー17段の壁として積み上げます。親（東）がサイコロ2個を振って壁を崩す位置を決め、全員に13枚を配ります。親は14枚目を取り、最初に捨てます。
オンラインでは、壁の構築と配牌は自動で行われます——手牌の管理だけをすればよいのです。

sections.heading: 自分の番
body: 自分の番では、1枚引き、手牌を確認し、1枚を表向きで捨てます。常に13枚を持ちます。捨てた牌は中央に置かれ、全員が見える——そして全員があなたの戦略を読めるようになります。
引いて捨てるリズムはすべてのルールで同じなので、スキルはルール間で活かせます。

sections.heading: 面子を作る：ポン・チー・カン
body: 他のプレイヤーが捨てた牌が手牌の面子を完成させるとき、引く代わりに鳴けます：
• ポン——同じ牌3枚。どのプレイヤーからでも鳴ける。
• チー——一つのスートの連続3枚。左隣のプレイヤーからのみ鳴ける。
• カン——同じ牌4枚。最も強力な鳴きで、一部のルールではボーナス牌を得られる。
鳴くと手牌が晒されます。開いた手牌は多くの点数システムで弱くなるため、初心者は鳴きは控えめにしましょう。

sections.heading: 和了形
body: 和了形は四面子一雀頭です。ツモで和了するか、他のプレイヤーの捨て牌を取ってロンします。
ルールによって最低点数も必要：香港スタイルは3飜、日本リーチは1役、中国公式は8点。最低点数に届かない完成形は和了にならず——手牌を改善し続けます。

sections.heading: 主要ルールの比較
body: • 香港麻雀——最も易しい入門点。最低3飜、寛容な点数計算、日本以外で最も広くプレイされているスタイル。
• 日本リーチ——競技の標準。門前手牌とリーチ宣言は高得点。厳格な役の要件。
• 中国公式（MCR）——国際大会ルール。最低8点は本格的な手牌構造を要求。
• アメリカ／台湾／四川——ジョーカー、16枚、字牌なしなど、地域ごとのバリエーション。
香港から始めましょう。安定して和了できるようになったら、リーチで深みを、中国公式で構造を学びましょう。

sections.heading: 無料で試す
body: ルールを読むだけでは限界があります——最も早い学び方は、実際に打つことです。香港麻雀の卓では、三人のコンピューター対戦相手と対局でき、聴牌ヒントと毎局の完全な点数内訳付き。完全無料、ブラウザで、ダウンロード不要です。

faq.question: 麻雀のルールを覚えるのにどれくらいかかりますか？
faq.answer: 基本の流れ——引く、捨てる、四面子一雀頭を作る——は約1時間で学べます。点数と戦略はもう少し時間がかかりますが、香港ルールは打ちながら学べるほど優しいです。

faq.question: 麻雀には四人必要ですか？
faq.answer: 対面ではそうです。オンラインではいつでもコンピューター対戦相手とプレイできます——一人でプレイしても、常に三人のボットが座ります。

faq.question: ポンとチーの違いは？
faq.answer: ポンは同じ牌3枚で、どのプレイヤーからでも鳴けます。チーは一つのスートの連続3枚で、左隣のプレイヤーからのみ鳴けます。

faq.question: 麻雀は勝つのが難しいですか？
faq.answer: ルールはシンプル。上手く勝つには練習が必要。早めに方向を決め、鳴きすぎない——この二つの習慣が最も早く結果を改善します。

mahjong-tiles-meaning-guide.title: 麻雀牌の意味完全ガイド：すべての牌を理解する
mahjong-tiles-meaning-guide.description: 144枚の麻雀牌の意味とは？筒・索・万・風・三元牌・花牌を一つずつ解説し、記号の意味をまとめて説明します。

sections.heading: 144枚の牌を一覧で
body: 標準的な麻雀セットは144枚の牌で、数牌、字牌、ボーナス牌に分かれます。各牌はスート内で4枚ずつ（花牌と季牌は例外あり）存在するため、合わせや面子が可能になります。
以下のチャートで各グループを説明します。これらがゲームに深みを与え——常に自分の手牌、卓の牌、山に残っている牌を追いかけることになります。

sections.heading: 三種の数牌
body: • 萬子（萬、wan）——牌には漢数字1から9が描かれています。
• 索子（條、tiao）——牌には1から9本の竹が描かれています。
• 筒子（筒、tong）——牌には1から9の銭または丸が描かれています。
各スートには各数字4枚ずつ、計36枚、数牌は合計108枚。順子は同じスートの連続3枚なので、スートは見た目以上に重要です。

sections.heading: 風牌
body: 四風は東・南・西・北です。字牌であり、順子は作れず刻子のみ可能。多くのルールでは、自風または場風の刻子で追加点数が入ります。
親は常に東で、順番は南・西・北と回ります。風牌は卓上の何かと対応する唯一の字牌です。

sections.heading: 三元牌
body: 三元牌は中（Red）、發（Green）、白（White）です。風牌と同様、刻子のみ作れますが、三元牌の刻子はほぼすべてのルールで得点になります——中の刻子は最低点数到達の最も確実な方法の一つです。
三種すべての三元牌刻子を揃えた手牌は、多くのゲームで大きな得点役です。

sections.heading: 花牌と季牌
body: 花牌と季牌は一部のルールで使われるボーナス牌です。各プレイヤーに花牌1枚、季牌1枚があり、自分のものを引くとボーナス点が入り、山から代わりの牌を引けます。
通常はすぐに脇に置き、和了形には含めません。

sections.heading: 牌の意味が重要な理由
body: 絵柄をすべて覚える必要はありません——数字とスートにすべての情報が含まれています。ただ、各牌の価値（順子に使える？刻子に使える？得点役になる？）を知ることで、ランダムな引きが計画に変わります。
牌に慣れれば、麻雀の残りはパターン認識とタイミングです。

faq.question: 麻雀牌には何種類ありますか？
faq.answer: 34種類の牌（萬子9、索子9、筒子9、風牌4、三元牌3）があり、ほとんど4枚ずつで144枚。花牌と季牌を含むセットでは8枚追加。

faq.question: 三スートは何を表していますか？
faq.answer: 萬子、索子、筒子は、ゲームの歴史的な中国起源における異なる硬貨の単位を表します。プレイ上は1〜9の三スートです。

faq.question: 字牌で順子は作れますか？
faq.answer: いいえ。風牌と三元牌は刻子のみ作れ、順子は作れません。孤立した字牌は通常早めに捨てる理由です。

faq.question: 最も価値のある牌は？
faq.answer: 単一の最も価値ある牌はありません——価値は手牌とルール次第。三元牌刻子、自風、1と9などの稀な数牌が一般的に最も有用です。

american-vs-chinese-mahjong.description: アメリカ麻雀と中国麻雀は実際には別のゲームです。ジョーカー、年次カード、計算、牌数を比較して、どちらが自分に合うか確認しましょう。

sections.heading: 同じ名前の二つのゲーム
body: どちらも麻雀牌を使い、四人でプレイしますが、1920年代に麻雀が西洋に渡った後、アメリカ麻雀と中国麻雀は大きく分岐しました。カード主導のアメリカ麻雀は手牌構築レースに近く、中国スタイルは本来の引き捨ての純粋さを保っています。
実際の違いを整理し、自分に合うスタイルを選べるようにします。

sections.heading: ハンドカード vs 固定の役
body: アメリカ麻雀の最大の特徴は、全米麻雀リーグが毎年発行する年次ハンドカードです。数十の正確な和了形がリストされ、それらのいずれかを正確に作らなければ和了できません。パターンは毎年変わるため新鮮さは保たれますが、牌だけではすべてのルールを把握できません。
中国麻雀は清一色、刻子、三元牌など、一世紀変わらない固定的な得点役を使います。北京でもオンラインでも、ルールは同じです。

sections.heading: ジョーカーとチャールストン
body: アメリカ麻雀は任意の牌の代わりになるジョーカーを使い、左・右・向かい合って牌を渡す固定の開局交換「チャールストン」を行います。どちらも中国麻雀には存在しない交換フェーズを加えます。
中国スタイルにはジョーカーも交換もありません——配られた牌だけで厳密にプレイします。

sections.heading: 牌、巡目、鳴き
body: アメリカ麻雀には花牌と季牌が含まれ、独自の鳴きルールがあります。中国麻雀（および地域バリエーション）は、定番のポン・チー・カンと引き捨ての構造を維持しています。
日本リーチと中国公式は独自の要素——リーチ宣言、8点最低——を加えますが、元の中国ゲームと同じ系統として認識できます。

sections.heading: どちらをプレイすべき？
body: 交換、ジョーカー、年次メタゲームのあるゲームが好きなら、アメリカ麻雀は素晴らしい社交的趣味です。国や大会を超えて通用する定番の競技ゲームが欲しいなら、中国麻雀——まず香港スタイル、次にリーチや中国公式——がより良い道です。
中国麻雀は今すぐ無料でオンライン対局でき、世界の残りの地域がプレイするゲームを教えてくれます。

faq.question: アメリカ麻雀と中国麻雀は同じ牌を使いますか？
faq.answer: 牌セットはおおむね同じですが、アメリカ麻雀はジョーカーと年次ハンドカードに依存し、中国麻雀は使いません。ゲームプレイの方が牌より大きく異なります。

faq.question: どちらが覚えやすい、アメリカか中国か？
faq.answer: 中国麻雀は役が固定で普遍的なため、ルールがより発見しやすい。アメリカ麻雀は毎年変わる年次ハンドカードの学習が必要です。

faq.question: アメリカ麻雀に年次ハンドカードは必要ですか？
faq.answer: はい——カードがその年の和了形を定義します。カードなしではアメリカルールで有効な和了を宣言できません。

faq.question: 中国麻雀を無料でオンライン対局できますか？
faq.answer: はい。香港麻雀の卓は無料、ブラウザで、定番の引き捨てゲームをコンピューター対戦相手と教えてくれます。

sections.heading: 選び方のポイント

sections.heading: 牌の素材：ベークライト、樹脂など
body: クラシックなセットは骨と竹製ですが、現代のセットは樹脂、プラスチック、メラミンを使います。良質な樹脂牌ははっきりした塗装面があり、擦れにくい。安いプラスチック牌は角が欠け、色が褪せることがあります。
最初のセットには、単色の樹脂またはメラミン牌で裏がすりガラス調のものを選びましょう——シャッフルしやすく、何年も持ちます。

body: 硬いケースやバッグは牌を保護し、ゲーム間の卓をきれいに保ちます。牌の種類ごとに仕切りのあるケースを選ぶと、次のゲームのセットアップが劇的に速くなります。
折りたたみ式のプレイマットは価値ある追加品：牌の滑りを防ぎ、卓面を保護します。

sections.heading: おすすめアクセサリー

sections.heading: 買う前に試す
body: 物理セットがまだ合うかわからない？コンピューター対戦相手と無料でオンライン学習できます——多くの物理セットが想定している香港麻雀とまったく同じルール——ハマったらセットを購入しましょう。

faq.question: 初心者向けセットには何枚必要ですか？

faq.question: 初心者に最適な牌サイズは？
faq.answer: 34mm牌がカジュアルプレイヤーに最も快適。28mmの大会用牌より大きく読みやすい。

faq.question: 高価な麻雀セットは価値がありますか？
faq.answer: 最初のセットには不要。はっきりした牌面の中級樹脂セットで十分。よく打つとわかってからアップグレードしましょう。

faq.question: 花牌と季牌は必要ですか？

mahjong-scoring-system-explained.title: 麻雀の点数計算を解説：飜と点数
mahjong-scoring-system-explained.description: 麻雀の点数計算とは？香港の飜、日本の飜、MCRの点数——一般的な役と手の価値を分かりやすく解説。

sections.heading: すべてのルールに最低点数がある
body: すべての麻雀ルールで、和了には最低点数に達する必要があります。名称は異なります——香港では飜、リーチでは飜（han）、中国公式ではポイント——ですが、考え方は同じ：手牌に十分な構造がなければ和了にならない。
この最低点数があるから、すべての手牌が最初の完成形争いの退屈なレースにならないのです。

sections.heading: 基本的な和了形
body: 基礎は常に四面子一雀頭。面子は刻子か順子。その上に役が価値を加えます：
• 清一色——一つのスートの牌だけ。
• 対々和——すべての面子が刻子。
• 断幺九——1・9・字牌なし。
• 三元牌の刻子——手牌に三元牌3種。
• 七対子——多くのルールで認められる代替和了形。

sections.heading: 香港の飜
body: 香港スタイルは最低3飜が必要。一般的な役とその価値：純全帯（清一色に近い純粋な一スート手、3飜）、対々和（3飜）、断幺九（1飜）、三元牌刻子（1〜3飜）。役は重なります——清一色に三元牌刻子があれば、どちらか単独より高得点。
点数表はきれいで意図的な手牌を評価します。安い手牌は確実だが遅い。野心的な手牌は大得点だが、そろうことは稀です。

sections.heading: 日本の飜とリーチ
body: リーチの点数計算は、飜の上に役（固定パターン）を加えます。リーチ自体が役——聴牌で宣言すると1飜加算され、このルールの象徴です。門前手牌ははるかに高得点で、忍耐を評価します。
リーチでも聴牌（テンパイ）の位置が重要：リーチを宣言するか、黙って別の得点を狙うか。飜を理解することが選択の鍵です。

sections.heading: 中国公式のポイント（MCR）
body: 中国公式は8点最低で、1点から88点までの大きな役カタログがあります。清一色、対々和、最も稀な役はすぐに積み上がります。
高い最低点数は本格的な構造を要求——七対子や清一色が通常必要で、MCRプレイヤーは最初の牌から手牌を計画します。

sections.heading: 卓に点数計算を任せる
body: オンラインでプレイすると、卓が点数を計算し、各和了後にどこから何点付いたかを正確に説明します。点数表を学ぶ最も早い方法——作った役と得た点数を、局ごとに確認できます。

faq.question: 飜、han、ポイントの違いは？
faq.answer: 和了形の役に付く点数という同じ考え方で、名称が異なります。香港は飜、リーチは飜（han）、中国公式はポイント。

faq.question: 麻雀で和了に必要な点数は？
faq.answer: 香港は3飜、日本リーチは最低1役、中国公式は8点。各ルールが独自の最低点数を定義します。

faq.question: 麻雀の点数を学ぶ最も簡単な方法は？
faq.answer: 卓が各点数を計算・説明するオンラインでプレイ。各和了後の内訳を見ることで、表を暗記するよりはるかに早く役を学べます。

faq.question: 最も高得点の役は？
faq.answer: 稀で構造の整った手牌が最高得点：清一色、対々和、七対子や国士無双などの特殊形が最高値の役の一つ。

faq.question: 最も人気のある麻雀の種類は？
faq.answer: 香港スタイルが日本以外で最も広くプレイされ、日本リーチが競技プレイを支配。中国では四川と中国公式が人気。

faq.question: 初心者に最も易しいスタイルは？
faq.answer: 香港麻雀。最低3飜と寛容な点数計算が、リーチや中国公式に進む前の最も優しい入門点。

faq.question: すべての麻雀バリエーションは四人でプレイしますか？
faq.answer: はい、四人ゲームが標準。麻雀ソリティアが例外——一人用パズルで、麻雀バリエーションではありません。

faq.question: 麻雀の種類ごとに異なる牌が必要ですか？
faq.answer: 標準144枚セットは香港、リーチ、中国公式に対応。アメリカ麻雀にはジョーカーが必要。台湾と四川には独自の慣習があります。

faq.question: 中国麻雀と日本麻雀の主な違いは？
faq.answer: 和了の門です。中国系は点数やファンの下限があり、形が整えば点数さえ足りれば和了できます。日本リーチは少なくとも一つの役が必要で、最初の捨牌から組み方が変わります。

faq.question: 同じ牌セットで違う麻雀を遊べる？
faq.answer: 通常ははい。香港・リーチ・中国公式・台湾は144牌セットを使い、花牌・季牌の扱いが異なります。アメリカ麻雀は年次カードがジョーカーと152牌構成を前提とする例外です。

faq.question: 四川麻雀はなぜ血戦と呼ばれる？
faq.answer: 誰かが和了しても対局が止まらないからです。和了者が離れ、残りが同じ局を続け、三人が終わるか牌山が尽きるまで進みます。一局に複数の勝者が出て、最初に上がった人が必ずしも最大の勝者ではありません。

mahjong-etiquette-tips.title: 麻雀のマナー：卓上の暗黙のルール
mahjong-etiquette-tips.description: 麻雀のマナーを学ぶ——牌の扱い方、いつ鳴くか、流れを読むこと、そして卓を和やかに保つ社交のルール。

sections.heading: マナーがゲームを可能にする
body: 麻雀は社交ゲームです。暗黙のルールは、全員が卓を読み、静かに考え、セッションを楽しめるように存在します。ほとんどはシンプル：巡目順を守る、自分の牌だけを触る、他のプレイヤーを急かさない。

sections.heading: 牌を丁寧に扱う
body: 1枚ずつ引き、1枚ずつ捨てる。牌を卓上に掃き散らさない。他のプレイヤーの捨て牌を並べ替えない。オンラインでは：ゲームを引き延ばさず自分の番を打つ——遅くても着実なプレイヤーは、速くて雑なプレイヤーより良い。

sections.heading: 自信を持って鳴き、習慣ではなく
body: 牌を鳴くことは手牌を卓に知らせること。マナー（と良い戦略）では、牌が本当に役立つときだけ鳴くべきです。繰り返し鳴いて弱い牌を捨てるのは未熟さの表れで、卓に無料の情報を与えます。

sections.heading: 牌だけでなく流れを読む
body: 捨て牌のリズムを見守る。捨てる前に止まるプレイヤーは決断中——通常は和了に近い。終盤の緊張を尊重し、危険な牌を捨てる前に考えましょう。

sections.heading: 勝っても負けても潔く
body: 勝ち負けはセッションの一部。和了牌を出したプレイヤーに礼を言い、不運な敗北にこだわらない。友好的なゲームでは、目的はスコアではなくセッションそのものです。

sections.heading: オンラインのマナー
body: オンラインでも同じルール：素早く巡目を打ち、誠実にプレイし、ボットは辛抱強いが人間はそうではないことを忘れない。当サイトの卓は止まらず、ペースを評価しません——良い習慣を学ぶ理想的な場所です。

faq.question: 他のプレイヤーの捨て牌を見てもいいですか？
faq.answer: はい——捨て牌はすべてのルールで公開情報。読むことは許可されているどころか、期待されています。

faq.question: 自分の番に時間をかけるのは失礼ですか？
faq.answer: 合理的な間は問題ありません。特に終盤。マナーの問題は引き延ばしや急かすこと。多くのカジュアル卓はペースに寛容です。

faq.question: 鳴きは宣言すべきですか？
faq.answer: はい——ポン、チー、カンをはっきり宣言し、卓が反応できるように。オンライン卓は自動で行います。

faq.question: 最も重要なマナールールは？
faq.answer: ゲームの流れを尊重すること：巡目順に打ち、捨て牌をきれいに保ち、局が終わるまで他のプレイヤーの牌や自分の牌を晒さない。

faq.question: 安い麻雀セットは買う価値がありますか？
faq.answer: たまに打つなら予算セットで十分。144枚であることを確認し、塗装と裏面一致に関するレビューをチェック。

mahjong-history-cultural-guide.title: 麻雀の歴史：清朝中国から世界へ
mahjong-history-cultural-guide.description: 麻雀の魅力的な歴史——19世紀中国での誕生、1920年代の西洋ブーム、日本とアメリカでの再発明、そして現在の地位。

sections.heading: 清朝中国での起源
body: 麻雀は19世紀半ばの中国、おそらく上海または寧波付近で生まれました。以前の中国の牌ゲームのロジックを借り、牌という形式に翻訳——多くの賭博ゲームの禁止を生き延びる形式です。
1890年代には上海の茶館の定番となり、交易路に沿って外へ広がりました。

sections.heading: 1920年代の西洋ブーム
body: 麻雀は1920年代初頭にアメリカに到達し、本物の社会現象——「麻雀ブーム」——となりました。数十万セットが売れ、アメリカのプレイヤーはすぐに独自の慣習を発明しました。チャールストンや後の年次ハンドカードなど。
中国ゲームは日本にも渡り、現在競技プレイを支配するリーチルールに洗練されました。

sections.heading: 地域ごとの再発明
body: 麻雀が広がるにつれ、多くのゲームになりました。日本は厳格な役と門前得点のリーチを構築。台湾は16枚ゲームを発展。四川は高速な「血戦」バリエーションを創出。アメリカは元のゲームから最も乖離したカード主導スタイルを維持。
各バージョンは引き捨ての核心を保ちながら、地域の好みに合わせて点数と戦略を再構築しました。

sections.heading: 今日の競技麻雀
body: 21世紀は競技麻雀をもたらしました：プロリーチリーグ、国際プレイ向け麻雀競技ルール（MCR）、世界中のオンラインシーン。麻雀はeスポーツに近いイベントやストリーミングにも登場し、新世代に届いています。
今日、ゲームはほぼすべての大陸で、クラブ、オンラインプラットフォーム、家庭でプレイされています。

sections.heading: 麻雀の文化的意味
body: 東アジアでは、麻雀はゲーム以上のもの——社交の儀式です。家族は祝日に卓を囲み、ゲームは世代を超える共通の絆です。西洋では異なる重みを持ち、エキゾチックの象徴から愛される趣味へと変わりました。
その二重の生——深く伝統的でありながら無限に適応可能——こそが、麻雀が生き残り広がった理由です。

sections.heading: 歴史をプレイする
body: 上海、日本、世界を席巻した同じ定番ゲームを——無料で、オンラインで、三人のコンピューター対戦相手と——プレイできます。目にする牌は、約二世紀前からプレイヤーが引いてきた同じ牌です。

faq.question: 麻雀はどこで発明されましたか？
faq.answer: 19世紀半ばの中国、おそらく上海または寧波付近で、以前の中国牌ゲームを牌に翻訳して生まれました。

faq.question: 麻雀はなぜ西洋で人気になったのですか？
faq.answer: 1920年代の「麻雀ブーム」がアメリカに流行の社交ゲームとして持ち込み、西洋のプレイヤーはチャールストンや年次ハンドカードなど独自のバリエーションを発展させました。

faq.question: 麻雀はどこでも同じゲームですか？
faq.answer: いいえ。中国、日本、アメリカ、台湾、四川麻雀は、牌・引き・捨ての核心を共有する別ゲームです。

faq.question: 麻雀はどのくらい古いですか？
faq.answer: 約150年。19世紀半ばの中国で生まれ、採用したすべての文化によって再発明されてきました。

how-to-play-american-mahjong.title: How to Play American Mahjong: Complete Beginner Guide
how-to-play-american-mahjong.description: American mahjong is not the game in Chinese mahjong guides. Learn the 152-tile set, the Charleston, jokers, the annual NMJL card, dead hands and how scoring really works — with a full walkthrough of your first hand.

sections.heading: American Mahjong Is a Different Game
body: American mahjong uses the same tiles you have seen in Chinese mahjong, and almost none of the same rules. In the Chinese game you win by building four sets and a pair. In the American game you win by matching one exact hand printed on a card that the National Mah Jongg League reissues every spring — and if your fourteen tiles do not match a line on that card, they are worth nothing at all.

Three things separate the two games. The card decides what is legal this year. Jokers, eight wild tiles that exist in no other variant, stand in for tiles inside a group of three or more. And the Charleston — a round of passing tiles before the first draw — lets every player steer their hand before luck takes over. Everything else in this guide grows out of those three.

sections.heading: The Tiles: 152, Not 144
body: An American set holds 152 tiles. The numbered tiles are the same as everywhere else: three suits — craks (characters), bams (bamboo) and dots — each running from one to nine with four copies of every tile, 108 in total. American players almost always use the short names, so a "three bam" is what a Chinese player calls a three of bamboo. The suits are colour-coded on the tile faces themselves — characters in red and black, bamboo in green, dots in a mix of blues and reds — but the colours printed on the card mean something else entirely, and mixing the two up is a standard first-week mistake.

The count changes in the honours. Sixteen winds (four each of East, South, West and North), twelve dragons (four Red, four Green, four White), eight flowers and eight jokers. Sixteen plus twelve plus eight plus eight is forty-four, and 108 plus 44 is 152 — the jokers are the eight tiles a Chinese set does not have at all.

Two of those tiles change how the game feels. Flowers are not set aside and scored the way they are in Chinese play; they are passed during the Charleston and used inside the hands that call for them. And jokers are wild, but only inside groups. There is also no chow in American mahjong — no runs of three consecutive tiles. Chinese players reach for that move by habit in their first American game, and it is not there. What replaces it is the quint: five identical tiles in a single group, a shape that cannot be completed without jokers and that gets its own section of the card.

sections.heading: You Cannot Win Without the Card
body: Every spring the National Mah Jongg League publishes a new card, and every spring it is different. A card lists somewhere between 65 and 75 legal hands, grouped into sections by theme — the year itself, 2468, Quints, Consecutive Run, 13579, Winds and Dragons, 369, and Singles and Pairs. You may build any hand on that card. You may build nothing else. The card is published by the league and sold each spring rather than shipped with any set, which is why a second-hand set on a resale site so often has everything except the one thing you actually need.

Read a line the way you read a recipe. Numbers are literal, with one exception: a zero stands for the White Dragon, which American players call the soap. The letter F is a flower and D is a dragon. Colour carries meaning — two tiles printed in the same colour must come from the same suit, and two tiles in different colours must come from different suits. You choose which suits to use, and that choice is most of your strategy.

This is why American players say the game is relearned every year. A hand that was legal last April may not exist this April. For your first session, do not try to learn the card. Pick two lines that use three or four groups, prop the card next to your rack, and play only those.

sections.heading: The Charleston: Three Passes Before Anyone Draws
body: Before the first draw, every player passes tiles. The first Charleston is mandatory and always runs in the same direction: three tiles to the player on your right, three across the table, three to the player on your left. Nine tiles leave your hand and nine arrive before a single tile is drawn from the wall. In practice you pass the three tiles that fit nothing you are holding, and you hope the nine coming back are less random than the nine going out.

A second Charleston may follow in the reverse direction — left, across, right — but any player may stop it, and in most groups someone does. During that second pass you may also make a blind pass, sending on tiles you have just received without looking at them, which helps when everything you have been handed is wrong for the hand you are chasing.

One rule catches everybody: jokers cannot be passed. They stay in your rack through the whole exchange. After the Charleston you and the player opposite may agree a courtesy pass of up to three tiles, and that number is negotiated rather than fixed — you may ask for three and receive none. The Charleston exists only in American mahjong, and it is the reason two players who start with similar tiles can end up in completely different hands.

sections.heading: Setting Up: Walls, Dice and Racks
body: All 152 tiles go face down and get shuffled, then each player builds a wall in front of their rack — nineteen tiles long and two tiles high, 38 to a side. Dice decide who is East, and East rolls again to decide where the wall is broken. Two dice produce the total, and that total fixes both who deals and where the wall is broken. Online it happens without you noticing; in person it is the moment everyone leans in to check the count.

Tiles are dealt from the broken wall in fours. East ends up with fourteen and everyone else with thirteen, and each player stands their tiles on a rack with the faces toward them. The rack is not decoration: it keeps a hand private in a game whose tiles are tall enough to be read from across the table.

East discards first, and play then moves counter-clockwise around the table. A turn is a draw and a discard, exactly as in Chinese mahjong. What differs is what you are allowed to do with the tiles other people throw away, and that is where the game turns.

sections.heading: Jokers: Where They Fit and Where They Never Fit
body: A joker is a wild tile, and it is the most misused tile in the game. It can stand in for any tile you need inside a group of three or more — a pung of three, a kong of four, a quint of five. Where a hand offers you a choice of suits, the joker takes whichever suit you choose.

What a joker cannot do is just as firm. It cannot stand in for a pair. It cannot stand in for a single tile. It cannot be used inside NEWS, the grouping of one of each wind, or inside the year numbers, because those groupings are about specific tiles rather than interchangeable ones. This one restriction kills more beginner hands than any other rule, because a pair looks exactly like a group that is one tile short. Picture two Red Dragons in your rack with a joker beside them. That is a pair plus a spare tile, not a pung — and if you lay it down as one, you have exposed a group the card does not recognise.

There is one escape hatch, and you should know it before somebody uses it on you. If a player exposes a group containing a joker, any player may swap for it: you hand over the real tile the joker is standing in for, add one extra tile from your hand as compensation, and the joker comes to you. You cannot take a joker out of a group just to keep it. The swap has to be paid for.

sections.heading: Exposing a Hand: Calling and the C on the Card
body: You may claim a discard to complete a group of three or more, and you must then lay that group face-up on your rack. You cannot claim a discard to make a pair — with one exception, which is claiming the tile that wins the hand outright.

Every hand on the card is marked either X or C. X means exposed: you may call discards freely while building it. C means concealed: you may not call anything except the tile that completes your hand, and the rest stays hidden on your rack until the end. Concealed hands are harder to finish and they pay more. The gap is deliberate: a C hand cannot be fed by the table, so the card pays you for building it blind.

Exposure is a commitment, not a convenience. The moment you lay a group down it is fixed, the table can see what you are chasing, and any joker inside it becomes available to whoever wants to pay for the swap. If that group turns out to belong to no line on the card, you have not simply given away information — you have killed the hand.

sections.heading: Dead Hands and the Two Ways Beginners Reach Them
body: A dead hand is a hand that can no longer win, whatever you draw. It happens when the tiles you have exposed match no line on the card, or when your hand holds the wrong number of tiles. A dead hand keeps drawing and discarding until somebody else wins, but it cannot win itself.

Beginners reach a dead hand the same two ways almost every time. The first is exposing a group that fits no line — usually because two lines were being chased at once and the group belonged to neither. The second is declaring a win with the wrong count: fourteen tiles for most hands, more for hands built on kongs or quints, and a hand that is one tile off is simply a hand that has not won.

The cure is boring and it works. Before you lay a group down, put a finger on the line you are building and read it back. If the group is on that line, expose it. If you cannot find it in three seconds, do not. Experienced players do this without thinking, which is why they rarely go dead. And if you do go dead, the hand is not over — you keep drawing and discarding, and your job becomes making sure nobody wins off you. A dead hand that folds safely costs you nothing but time.

sections.heading: Scoring: Who Pays What
body: Every hand on the card carries a value, and the values run from roughly twenty-five to roughly seventy-five. That number is the size of the pot for that hand. The card decides it — not how well you played.
Only three things change what each player actually pays. Who threw the winning tile. Whether you drew it yourself. And whether your hand is jokerless.

Win on a discard and the player who threw it pays double while the other two pay face value. Draw the tile yourself and every player pays double. The total settles between you and each opponent rather than out of a central pot, which is why American players keep score on a slip of paper instead of stacking chips. Run it once and the shape of the game becomes clear: a thirty-point hand won on a discard pays sixty from the thrower and thirty from each of the other two, a hundred and twenty in total. Win the same hand on your own draw and all three opponents pay sixty, which comes to a hundred and eighty.

A jokerless hand — one built with no wild tiles at all — doubles what every opponent pays, except in the Singles and Pairs section, where jokers are barred anyway and the bonus would mean nothing. If the wall runs out before anyone completes a hand, that is a wall game: nobody wins, nobody pays, and the deal passes on.

sections.heading: Your First Session
body: Set the card where you can see it and pick two X hands that use three or four groups. X hands let you call tiles, which keeps the game moving while you learn. Ignore the point values on the first night and ignore Singles and Pairs completely — those hands are hard, and jokers are banned inside them. If you are learning alone, pick hands you can picture finishing in five turns. If you are learning at a table, say your target hand out loud for the first few deals — hearing a hand named is how most American players learned the card in the first place.

Play three or four hands before you decide anything about the game. The Charleston will feel chaotic for two of them, you will probably expose a group you should not have, and the card will take longer to read than you expect. After one evening it stops being a puzzle and becomes a shape you recognise.

faq.question: How many tiles are in an American mahjong set?
faq.answer: American mahjong is played with 152 tiles: 108 numbered tiles across three suits, 16 winds, 12 dragons, 8 flowers and 8 jokers. The eight jokers and eight flowers are what make an American set larger than the 144-tile Chinese set.

faq.question: What is the Charleston in American mahjong?
faq.answer: The Charleston is a mandatory round of passing tiles before the first draw. Each player passes three tiles to the right, three across and three to the left. A second Charleston in reverse is optional and any player may stop it. Jokers can never be passed.

faq.question: Can I use a joker for a pair in American mahjong?
faq.answer: No. A joker can only stand in for a tile inside a group of three or more — a pung, kong or quint. It can never substitute for a pair, a single tile, one of the four winds in NEWS, or a tile in the year numbers.

faq.question: Do I need a new mahjong card every year?
faq.answer: Yes. The National Mah Jongg League publishes a new card each spring with a different set of legal hands, and only the current card is valid. Older cards describe hands that no longer exist, so they cannot be used at a table playing the current year.

faq.question: What is a dead hand?
faq.answer: A dead hand cannot win, no matter what you draw. It usually comes from exposing a group that matches no line on the card, or from holding the wrong number of tiles. You keep playing the hand out, but you cannot win it yourself.

faq.question: Is American mahjong harder than Chinese mahjong?
faq.answer: It is harder to start and easier to master. You cannot win by building any sensible shape — you have to match a line on the card, which takes a few sessions to read fluently. But with no chows and a fixed list of hands, there are fewer patterns to learn than in Chinese play.

faq.question: Can I play American mahjong online for free?
faq.answer: Yes. Our tables deal a full hand against computer opponents, track the wall and score every win for you, so you can learn the card and the Charleston without needing three other players at the table.

how-many-players-mahjong.title: How Many Players Can Play Mahjong? 2, 3 and 4-Player Setups
how-many-players-mahjong.description: Mahjong is built for four players, but you can play tonight with two or three. Learn exactly what changes: the wall, claiming, the Charleston, sanma, Siamese racks, which tiles to remove, and how scoring adjusts.

sections.heading: Why Four Players Became the Standard
body: Mahjong is written for four. The wall is built in four sides, the seats are named after the four winds, and the rule that a hand needs four sets and a pair quietly assumes there are four hands in play. Four is also the number the game needs to work as a game of information: with three opponents reading a shared discard pile, every tile you throw away is a signal and every tile you keep is a hint you cannot help giving. Change the count and you change how much information is in the room, which is the real variable in every adaptation below.

None of that makes four mandatory. Mahjong adapts to two, three or five players with small mechanical changes — you remove tiles or seats, you change who may claim a discard, and occasionally you change what counts as a win. What follows is exactly what moves in each case, so you can sit down tonight with whoever is actually available.

sections.heading: What Actually Changes When a Seat Is Empty
body: Four things move when a seat goes empty, and only one of them is obvious. The tiles that seat would have drawn stay in the wall. Whoever would have passed you tiles in the Charleston is gone. The number of players who can claim a discard drops. And the number of people who pay you when you win drops with it.

The wall is the change players feel first. Four players take 52 tiles into their hands before play begins; three players take 39. That leaves more tiles in the wall, which sounds like an advantage and mostly is — hands finish instead of stalling, because the wall runs dry far less often. Three-player games end in an actual win more frequently than four-player ones, and they end sooner. Do the division and the reason is plain: a four-player hand gives each player roughly twenty-one draws, and a three-player hand gives each of them about thirty.

The change you notice last is the information. Three opponents means three people reading your discards and three hands competing for the tiles you need; two opponents means half as many eyes on you and the tiles you want concentrated in fewer hands. Fewer players does not make the game easier. It makes it more direct, which is why three-handed mahjong is usually faster and more aggressive than the game you are used to.

sections.heading: Three Players, American Style
body: American mahjong allows three-handed play, and the simplest adaptation is to skip the Charleston entirely. There are no passes at all, the dealer discards first, and play begins immediately. For a game whose opening ritual is a nine-tile exchange, dropping it changes more than it sounds — you start with the hand you were dealt and no chance to repair it.

The alternative that most groups actually use is a ghost seat. A fourth hand is dealt face down and never played, but it still takes part in the Charleston, with tiles passing to and from a wall nobody draws from. This keeps the exchange intact and keeps the table’s rhythm, at the cost of three passes’ worth of tiles that vanish out of the game. Setup takes one extra step: deal the ghost hand as though a fourth player were sitting there, leave it face down in front of the empty space, and pass to it on every leg of the Charleston. Nobody looks at it, and it never draws or discards.

Choose between them by what your table wants. Skip the Charleston if you want speed, a clean start and no bookkeeping. Use the ghost seat if the ritual is part of why you play — the passing, the reading of who gave you what, the small politics of a courtesy pass. Both are legal, and both are played in American clubs.

sections.heading: Three Players, Japanese Style: Sanma
body: Japanese three-player mahjong has a name, sanma, and it is not a house rule. It is a recognised variant with its own competitive scene, and in some parts of Japan it is played more than the four-player game.

Sanma removes the 2 through 8 of one suit — 28 tiles in total — leaving 108. The suit that gets cut is normally characters, which leaves the one and the nine sitting in a suit where nobody can build a run. What is left is a faster, more aggressive game: fewer tiles to read, more turns that matter, and a higher chance that any given discard is genuinely dangerous. A three-handed wall also stretches further per player than a four-handed one, which sounds like it should slow things down and does the opposite — more draws means more chances to complete, so sanma players push thinner hands than they would with four at the table.

Sanma also changes the furniture of the game. A drawn north wind often counts as a bonus tile rather than a usable seat wind, riichi gets declared more often because scoring is compressed, and hands run shorter from start to finish. If your group knows Japanese mahjong and is one player short, this is the variant to play — the rules are settled, so nobody has to argue about house rules at the table.

sections.heading: Two Players: The Draw-Only Duel
body: The simplest two-player game removes claiming altogether. Each player draws from the wall, decides, and discards. Nobody may pong, kong or chow another player’s discard. You are not so much playing against your opponent as racing them, and the first player to complete a hand wins it. Set it up by dealing thirteen tiles each and leaving the rest of the set in the wall; you need no ghost hand and no rulebook, because the only thing you removed is the right to claim.

This version is slower per hand and much better for learning. Because no discard can be claimed, every tile you need has to come off the wall, which means you spend the whole game reading your own hand and counting tiles instead of watching three discard rows. It is the fastest way to find out which shapes actually connect and which ones stall forever.

It also has a quiet tactical layer that four-player games rarely offer. With one opponent and no calling, the discards in front of them are the only information you have — and that information is complete. If both copies of a tile you need are already lying in their pile, you can abandon that hand before you waste ten turns chasing it.

sections.heading: Two Players: Siamese Racks
body: American mahjong has its own two-player format, usually called Siamese mah jongg, and it does not shrink the game — it doubles it. Each player runs two racks, 27 tiles in total, and has to complete two hands rather than one. There is no Charleston; you start from what you were dealt. Set the two racks one above the other and deal 27 tiles to each player — two hands’ worth — and the wall still holds close to a hundred tiles, so the game does not run dry before somebody finishes.

The interest is in choosing what to build. Before your first discard you are looking at 27 tiles and picking two lines off the card, and the temptation is to pick the two hands you like best. The better play is to pick two hands that share as few tiles as possible, so that a tile which helps one rack is not sitting useless in the other. You may move tiles between your racks freely while both are concealed; once a group is exposed, it belongs to that rack for good.

Two racks also change the endgame. You declare each completed hand separately, and the first declaration locks in its jokers — nobody can swap a joker out of a hand you have already declared. Winning both racks is the goal, and finishing one while your opponent finishes neither is usually enough to take the game.

sections.heading: What to Remove From the Set
body: Some variants take tiles out, and the arithmetic is worth knowing before you start pulling tiles off the table. Chinese three-player play usually drops the North wind: remove all four north tiles and you are down to 132, with the north seat simply not existing and north often treated as a bonus for whoever holds it.

Japanese sanma cuts far deeper, removing 28 tiles — the 2 through 8 of one suit — and leaving 108. The trade is that the wall gets thin relative to the number of players, which is part of why sanma hands run fast and finish often. You are not removing tiles to make the game harder; you are removing them to keep three hands from drawing dead. The rule of thumb is that tiles come out in multiples of four: four winds, or seven ranks across one suit. That is why the Chinese adjustment is four tiles and the Japanese one is twenty-eight.

Two-player games usually remove nothing at all. With half the hands in play, a standard set already leaves an unusually deep wall — 110 tiles against 26 held — so the game plays out instead of stalling, and cutting tiles would only make it end faster than it needs to.

sections.heading: Five Players and Beyond: Passing the Seat
body: Five players is easier than three, because nothing about the game changes. Four play a standard hand while one sits out, and the seat rotates so nobody sits out twice before everybody has. Many groups send out the player who came second in the previous hand; some send out the last-place finisher as a gentler penalty. The seated four play entirely normal mahjong — same wall, same Charleston, same claims, same scoring — and nothing at the table tells the fifth player they are not in a standard game.

Six players works the same way with two seats moving. The alternative — a five-player table where everybody plays — usually goes badly: five hands competing for the same 136 tiles means the wall runs down faster, draws get more frequent, and two players will spend most hands holding nothing that connects.

Rotating a seat is the only adaptation that changes no rule at all. Nobody removes tiles, nobody changes how claiming works, and the Charleston still runs with four players, because there are four. If your group is larger than four, this is the answer. The game was designed for exactly four people, and it rewards you for keeping it there.

sections.heading: How Scoring and Minimums Adjust
body: Fewer players means fewer people paying, and that changes the shape of a session more than any single rule. In a four-player game a win collects from three opponents. In a three-player game it collects from two, so the same card value moves a third less on the scorepad.

The honest fix is not to inflate the values but to count hands instead of a running total. Ten hands of three-player play is a session; ten hands of four-player play is a session too, and both are worth playing. Comparing raw totals across the two formats is the mistake, not the scoring.

The other lever is the minimum. Chinese and Japanese rulesets set a floor — three faan in Hong Kong, one yaku in riichi, eight points in Chinese Official — and that floor exists to stop players winning with a hand that is technically complete but strategically empty. With fewer players the same floor bites harder, because the wall is deeper and cheap hands are easier to assemble. If your three-player sessions feel slow, lower the minimum before you change anything else. One concrete version: drop the Hong Kong floor from three faan to two for a few hands and watch what happens — cheap hands start finishing, the wall stops running out, and hands per hour roughly doubles. That is a better trade than inflating every card value, which changes the arithmetic without changing how often anybody wins.

sections.heading: Which Setup Should You Play Tonight?
body: Two players: play the draw-only duel while you are learning, and Siamese racks once you know the card and want a real game. Three players: use a ghost seat if you are playing American and want the Charleston, sanma if you are playing Japanese and want a settled ruleset, or skip the Charleston if you simply want to start. Four players: play the standard game. Five or more: rotate the seat and play the standard game.

The player count was never the hard part. Every version above uses the same 136 or 152 tiles, the same draw-and-discard turn and the same four-sets-and-a-pair target. What changes is how much information you have and how many people are paying when somebody finally wins. If you are not sure which ruleset to learn first, Hong Kong mahjong is the gentlest entry point for a small table — its three-faan minimum lets you win with the shapes you are already building by accident. Pick the version that fits who is actually in the room, and play.

faq.question: How many players do you need for mahjong?
faq.answer: Four is standard, and it is what every ruleset assumes. You can play with two or three by adapting the setup, and with five or more by rotating one seat out between hands so that four players are always at the table.

faq.question: Can you play mahjong with 3 players?
faq.answer: Yes. In American mahjong the Charleston is usually skipped, or a ghost fourth hand is dealt to keep the passing sequence intact. Japanese mahjong has a formal three-player variant, sanma, that removes 28 tiles and is played competitively.

faq.question: Can 2 people play mahjong?
faq.answer: Yes. The simplest version lets players draw and discard only, with no claiming at all. American mahjong has its own two-player format called Siamese mah jongg, where each player runs two racks of 27 tiles and must complete two hands.

faq.question: What is sanma?
faq.answer: Sanma is Japanese three-player mahjong. It removes the 2 through 8 of one suit — 28 tiles — leaving 108 in play. The result is a faster, more aggressive game that is played competitively in Japan rather than treated as a casual workaround.

faq.question: Do you remove tiles in three-player mahjong?
faq.answer: Not always. American three-handed play keeps all 152 tiles and simply skips the Charleston or deals a ghost hand. Chinese three-player play commonly removes the four North wind tiles, leaving 132. Japanese sanma removes 28 tiles, leaving 108.

faq.question: Can 5 people play mahjong?
faq.answer: Yes, by rotating the seat. Four players play a standard hand while the fifth sits out, and the seat moves each hand so nobody sits out twice in a row. This changes no rule at all, which is why it works better than trying to play with five hands.

faq.question: Does the Charleston change with fewer players?
faq.answer: In American mahjong, yes. With three players you either skip the Charleston entirely or deal a ghost hand that takes part in the passing. Two-player Siamese mah jongg has no Charleston at all. Japanese and Chinese rulesets have no Charleston in any format.

mahjong-strategy.title: Mahjong Strategy: How to Actually Win More Hands
mahjong-strategy.description: A practical mahjong strategy guide: tile efficiency, hand value, reading discards, and when to push or fold. Every number verified against a real scoring engine.

sections.heading: Strategy Starts With One Question
body: Most mahjong advice is a list of tips. Tips are hard to use because they conflict: keep pairs, but do not keep too many pairs. Push for value, but do not push too long. Without a principle underneath, a beginner has no way to decide which tip applies to the hand in front of them.

There is a principle, and it is a single question. Every turn, ask: does this discard bring me closer to winning, or does it keep me safer? Those two goals pull in opposite directions, and almost every strategic decision in mahjong is a judgement about which one matters more right now. A hand that is close to winning justifies risk. A hand that is far away, late in the game, justifies caution.

Everything else in this guide is a tool for answering that question well. Tile efficiency tells you how close you are. Hand value tells you whether winning is worth the risk. Discard reading tells you how dangerous a tile is. Push-or-fold is the decision itself.

The order matters. Beginners usually learn hand value first, because scoring is concrete and visible on a score sheet. But efficiency comes first in practice, because a hand you never complete scores nothing regardless of what it was worth on paper. A low-value hand that finishes beats a high-value hand that stays in your rack.

This guide uses numbers verified against a real mahjong engine rather than rule-of-thumb figures. Where you see a wait count or a shanten figure, it came from evaluating that exact hand layout, not from estimating. That matters because intuitive tile-efficiency advice is frequently off by a tile or more, and a one-tile error compounds across a whole session.

sections.heading: Tile Efficiency: Closing the Gap
body: Shanten is the number of tile improvements between your hand and a winning shape. A hand at zero shanten is one tile away from completion and is called tenpai. A hand at shanten two needs two more useful draws. Every strategy decision starts by knowing this number.

The counting is less mysterious than it looks. A complete hand is four sets plus a pair. You count how many of those five blocks you already hold, then account for the partial blocks that can become sets. Run the engine on a hand of m2 m3 m4 m5 m6 m7 p2 p3 p4 s2 s3 s5 s5 and it reports shanten 0 with a two-sided wait on s1 or s4 — two complete sequences, one more sequence, and a pair, with one block still to finish.

The practical skill is not counting shanten by hand. It is recognising which block to keep when you must choose. Two blocks can look equally useful and differ substantially in how many tiles complete them.

Here is a comparison that surprises most beginners. Give two hands the same nine completed tiles, then give one the block 2-3 and the other the block 2-2. Both need one more tile to become a set. The engine reports three waits for the first and four for the second, because the pair can also serve as the pair in the finished hand, which frees the remaining block. Same tile count, different flexibility.

The gap widens with compound shapes. A hand holding 2-2-3-3 in one suit, with the rest of the hand complete, waits on six different tiles. Replace it with plain 2-3 and 4-5 and the same hand drops to three. The compound shape works as two overlapping partial sets, so it accepts tiles that complete it in either direction. This is the single most valuable shape to recognise, and it is invisible if you only ever think in terms of separate blocks.

sections.heading: Hand Value: Is Winning Worth It
body: Efficiency answers how close you are. Value answers whether being close is worth much. Both matter, because a fast hand and a valuable hand are usually not the same hand.

Value in mahjong comes from patterns rather than from tiles themselves. Sequences are easy to build and score little. Triplets are harder and score more. Keeping to one suit, or holding only simple tiles, or finishing on a self-drawn tile — each adds points, and each narrows the set of hands you can build.

The trade is real and it is usually worth taking in a specific direction. Chasing a high-value hand means accepting a hand you complete less often. Chasing speed means accepting a smaller payout when you do finish. Neither is right in the abstract; the choice depends on how far along the hand is and how much time the game has left.

A workable default for beginners: build efficiency first, then notice value when it arrives on its own. If three of your blocks happen to point at one suit, lean into it. If they are spread out, do not force them together. Forced value is the most common way beginners turn a hand that would have completed into one that never does.

There is also a defensive dimension to value, which beginners miss. A visible, valuable hand attracts attention. When you call tiles repeatedly and discard from a narrow range, the other three players read what you are building and start holding the tiles you need. A quieter hand that finishes unexpectedly often beats a loud hand that everyone has learned to block.

sections.heading: Reading Discards Like a Detective
body: Every tile a player discards is a public statement about what they do not need. Individually the statements are weak. In sequence they become a reliable portrait of a hand.

The first thing to read is suit concentration. A player discarding one suit early and rarely touching another is collecting that second suit. If their early discards are honours, they are likely building a hand that ignores honour tiles entirely. Either read tells you which of your own discards are dangerous.

The second thing to read is timing. An early discard of a middle tile is usually meaningless — they simply had it and did not want it. The same tile discarded late in the hand is a strong signal, because by then the player has had many turns to use it and chose not to. Late discards carry far more information than early ones.

The third is the gap pattern. If a player has discarded 4 and 6 of a suit, they probably do not hold 5, which makes 5 relatively safe against them. This is the basis of most defensive play, and it works because of a structural fact about mahjong: with four copies of every tile, visible tiles are gone tiles.

Applying these reads takes practice, and there is a shortcut for beginners. Rather than trying to model all three opponents at once, track the single player who has visibly committed — the one who has called tiles and is discarding from a narrow range. That player is the one most likely to win and the one whose waits are easiest to infer. Defend against them specifically and treat the other two as background.

sections.heading: Push or Fold: The Decision Itself
body: This is where the principle from the first section becomes an action. You are holding a hand that is not yet ready. A player across the table has called several tiles and is discarding in a suspiciously narrow pattern. Do you keep building, or do you start discarding only safe tiles and accept that this hand is over?

The honest answer is that this decision is about expected value, not about courage. Pushing means you might complete your hand and you might deal into theirs. Folding means you certainly do not win, but you also certainly do not pay. The question is which outcome loses less over many hands.

Three signals tilt the decision toward folding. Your hand is far from ready — the engine says two or more shanten, meaning you need multiple good draws, not one. The game is late, so the remaining draws are few. And the threatening player has shown strength, so the chance their hand is real is high.

Three signals tilt the other way. You are already tenpai, so a single tile finishes you and the threat may not get another turn. Your hand has value worth defending. Or the threatening player has been calling from an early stage and their hand is more likely to be cheap than dangerous.

The practical rule that captures most of this: fold early, push late — but only once ready. Folding a hand at shanten two costs almost nothing, because it was unlikely to complete anyway. Folding a finished hand at tenpai costs the whole hand. The mistake beginners make is the reverse, staying in with a hopeless hand early and then abandoning a live hand late out of nerves.

One more consideration that beginners consistently undervalue: not dealing in is itself a positive result. In most scoring systems a deal-in payment is larger than what you would have won with a small hand. Simply not paying can be worth more than winning, and the players who understand this are the ones who keep their scores steady across a long session.

sections.heading: Putting It Together in a Real Hand
body: Take a concrete hand and walk it forward. You hold m2 m3 m4 m5 m6 m7 p2 p3 p4 s2 s3 s5 s5. Three complete sequences, one pair, and the partial block s2-s3 to finish.

The engine evaluates this at shanten 0, waiting on s1 or s4 — a two-sided wait, the strongest common shape, because it accepts tiles from both ends of the block. Two complete sequences in one suit plus a partial block in another is the template fastest hand: several ways to finish, no single point of failure.

Now suppose someone discards p7 early. Irrelevant; you do not need dots. Suppose instead that the player to your left calls two tiles in dots and then discards a dot they had apparently held for a while. That is a signal, and the safe dodge is to keep your own dot discards to tiles already visible on the table.

Your wait is s1 or s4. Count what is visible. If two of the four s1 tiles are already discarded, the wait has narrowed to what remains. This is where counting four copies stops being an abstract fact and becomes a number you use: a two-sided wait on a tile with two copies visible is meaningfully worse than the same wait with nothing visible.

If the game reaches its final draws with your hand still at tenpai and the threatening player still pushing, you are in the spot the previous section described. Your hand is complete-adjacent, so folding wastes real equity. The correct play is usually to keep the wait and accept the risk, because a finished hand that pays is better than a safe hand that scores nothing.

That is the whole framework in miniature: measure the gap, notice the value, read the discards, then decide. None of the four steps is difficult alone. The skill is running them in order, every turn, without skipping to the decision first.

faq.question: What is the single most important mahjong strategy for beginners?
faq.answer: Tile efficiency. Knowing how many tiles away your hand is, and choosing the block that accepts the most completing tiles, improves results faster than any scoring tactic. A hand that completes beats a valuable hand that never does.

faq.question: Should I always keep pairs?
faq.answer: No. A pair is more flexible than a two-tile sequential block, because it can become a triplet or serve as the finished hand’s pair. But a hand with too many pairs loses the sequences it needs, so keep pairs that have a path and discard ones that do not.

faq.question: How do I know when to stop pushing and fold?
faq.answer: Fold when your hand is two or more shanten, the game is late, and an opponent has shown strength. Folding early is cheap; abandoning a finished hand is expensive. The common beginner error is doing the opposite.

faq.question: Is it worth chasing a valuable hand?
faq.answer: Only when the value arrives naturally. Build for efficiency first and lean into value when several of your blocks already point the same direction. Forcing a high-value shape usually means the hand never completes at all.

best-opening-hands.title: Best Mahjong Opening Hands: What to Keep in Your First Discards
best-opening-hands.description: Which starting tiles to keep and which to throw away first. Real shanten counts for the shapes that matter, plus the opening mistakes that quietly cost you the hand.

sections.heading: Your First Discards Decide the Hand
body: The opening is the part of mahjong where skill compounds fastest. A single early discard rarely matters, but the pattern of your first four or five discards sets the shape of everything that follows. Get them wrong and you spend the rest of the hand recovering. Get them right and the hand plays itself.

The reason the opening is so consequential is that it is the only point where you have maximum freedom and minimum information. All thirteen tiles are yours and nobody has shown anything. Every later decision is constrained by what you have already thrown and by what your opponents have revealed. The opening is the one moment you are choosing your hand rather than reacting to it.

So opening strategy is really about which shapes deserve to be kept. Some starting tiles are obviously disposable — isolated honours, tiles with no neighbours. Others look similar but differ sharply in how many future tiles they accept. This guide gives you the shanten counts for those shapes so the choice stops being a guess.

A useful frame before the details: a hand is four sets plus a pair, so thirteen tiles must eventually become those five blocks. In the opening you are not trying to complete anything. You are trying to hold five blocks that can each become something, and discarding the tiles that cannot belong to any of them.

There is a second reason the opening deserves separate study, and it is about mistakes rather than upside. Opening errors are the easiest to repeat unconsciously, because each individual discard is small and the feedback arrives many turns later. A player who habitually keeps isolated honours will never see a single turn where that choice visibly costs them. They will only see a general pattern of hands that never quite came together, and that pattern is much harder to diagnose than a single blunder.

One warning that applies throughout. These numbers describe tile layouts in isolation. They ignore what is visible on the table, what your opponents are doing, and what suit you are being handed by the draw. Use them to compare shapes, not as a formula to follow blind.

sections.heading: The Shapes Worth Keeping
body: Not all two-tile blocks are equal, and the differences are larger than most beginners assume. Given the same rest of the hand, three partial blocks accept different numbers of completing tiles: a two-sided block such as 2-3 accepts four tile types, a closed block such as 1-2 accepts four but from one end only, and a gap block such as 1-3 accepts four into the middle.

The wide-open block is the strongest simple shape. A block like 2-3 accepts 1 and 4, which is two tile types across two copies each, for four tiles’ worth of improvement. It also keeps more of the suit available, because 1 and 4 sit at opposite ends of the block rather than in the middle.

Pairs deserve their own mention because they are more flexible than their two tiles suggest. Run the engine on a hand whose remaining blocks are complete except for a 2-2 pair and it reports four waits; the same hand with a 2-3 block reports three. The pair can finish as a triplet or, if the rest of the hand provides one, serve as the pair the completed hand requires. That dual role is why pairs are worth keeping even when they look passive.

The most valuable shape in the opening is the compound block, and it is the one beginners consistently fail to recognise. Hold 2-2-3-3 in one suit and the engine reports six waits. Hold the equivalent 2-3 and 4-5 and the same hand reports three. The compound shape overlaps: it can develop toward two sequences, toward a triplet plus a sequence, or toward a pair plus a sequence, so it accepts tiles that help in any of those directions.

The practical upshot: when you see overlapping tiles in one suit, treat them as one asset rather than two separate problems. Their value is not the sum of their parts. It is the set of futures they allow.

There is a ranking worth memorising, from weakest to strongest, for the two-tile blocks you will see most often. A closed block pointing at the far end of a suit is weakest, because it accepts from one direction and the tiles it needs are near the edge where fewer shapes live. A gap block is better, since it accepts a specific middle tile from either side. A two-sided block is better still, accepting from both ends. A pair is roughly as flexible as a two-sided block but in a different way, and a compound overlapping shape beats all of them.

None of this means you should keep a weak block over a strong one in every case. The rest of the hand constrains the choice — a suit you already hold three sequences in has less room for a fourth, and a block in a suit you are largely ignoring is worth less than its raw flexibility suggests. What the ranking gives you is a default, and defaults are what you need in the opening when there is no other information to use.

sections.heading: The Shapes to Throw Away First
body: The mirror image of keeping good shapes is identifying dead tiles, and the opening is when they are easiest to spot. A tile is dead when no realistic path leads from it to a set plus a pair.

Isolated honours are the clearest case. A lone East wind has no neighbours, cannot form a sequence, and needs two more identical copies to become a triplet. Two of those copies might sit in other players’ hands or in the wall. Early in the hand it is the most disposable tile on the table, and discarding it first costs nothing.

Isolated terminals are the next to go. A lone 1 or 9 in a suit can only form a sequence one way, and only with two specific partners. Holding that 1 while the 2 and 3 never arrive is a tile you carried for nothing. Late in a session you will notice how often the tiles you finally throw away are the same isolated terminals you held at the start.

The subtle mistake is discarding a middle tile because it looks unconnected. A lone 5 has neighbours on both sides and can join blocks in four different directions. It looks like nothing and behaves like an asset. Beginners throw these and keep their lone honours, which is precisely backwards.

There is a timing rule that captures it: discard in order of shrinking options. Honours have the fewest paths, then terminals, then middle tiles. Following that order means you spend your early discards on the tiles that could never have helped, and reach the middle game still holding the tiles that still can.

One subtlety that catches players who have learned the rule: isolated honours are disposable, but a *pair* of honours is a completely different asset. Two identical winds can become a triplet with a single draw, which makes them a legitimate block, and a triplet of your seat wind or the round wind carries bonus value in many rulesets. The rule is about isolated tiles, not about honour tiles as a category. Discard the single East; keep the two of them.

The same distinction applies to terminals. An isolated 9 is nearly worthless. A pair of 9s is a valid block with a path to a triplet. Beginners who learn the terminal rule too literally will throw the second 9 and lose a real asset along with the dead one.

sections.heading: Counting Copies Changes Everything
body: There are exactly four of every mahjong tile, and every copy you can see is a copy that cannot complete your hand. This fact is worth using from the first discard, not just in the endgame.

The logic is straightforward. If a shape accepts a particular tile and all four copies are visible, that shape is dead and should be reassessed. If two are visible, the shape still works but at half strength. Two shapes that look equivalent can be far apart once you count.

Applying it early feels unnatural because the opening is when least is visible. But even the opening gives you information. Your own hand holds some copies, and the first few discards from each player are public. By the time you have thrown four tiles yourself, a meaningful fraction of the wall is accounted for.

There is a second-order version of this that separates strong players. Holding a tile that your own discard pattern suggests you do not want is a form of disguise, but holding a tile that is visibly scarce is simply a waste. If two copies of the tile your block needs are already discarded, that block is worth less than the same block in a suit where nothing is visible — and the correction belongs in your opening plan, not just your endgame.

The habit to build is counting the tiles that matter to your two or three live blocks. Not all 34 tile types, just the handful your hand is actually waiting on. That is a small enough number to track in your head while the hand is still developing.

A worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. Suppose your hand’s remaining path runs through the 3 and 6 of one suit, and you have seen two 3s and three 6s across the table. Your effective outs have dropped from eight tiles to three. The block is not dead, but it is running at under half strength, and a competing block in a suit where nothing is visible is now the better bet despite looking no different on your rack.

This is the calculation that separates a player who is reading the table from one who is merely looking at it. The tiles you cannot see are the only ones that can still help you, and their number changes every turn. Recalculating it is cheap; ignoring it means planning around tiles that no longer exist.

sections.heading: What a Strong Opening Looks Like
body: Put the pieces together and a strong opening has a recognisable profile. Several blocks are live, at least one is a two-sided shape, at least one pair is present or forming, and no tile is being carried without a path to a set.

A concrete example. Start with m2 m3 m4 m5 m6 m7 p2 p3 p4 s2 s3 s5 s5 and the engine places you at shanten 0, waiting on s1 or s4. That is a finished-quality hand from the opening — three sequences, a pair, and a two-sided block. It did not require cleverness. It required holding the right shapes while discarding everything else.

Compare a weaker opening with the same tile count: m1 m3 m5 m7 m9 p2 p4 p6 p8 s1 s3 s5 z1. Every tile is isolated, nothing overlaps, and the engine reports shanten 5. Hands like this are not unlucky. They are what remains when a player keeps tiles that only look useful — alternating numbers, one from each suit — instead of tiles that connect.
The difference between those two hands is not the draw. Both are legal thirteen-tile hands. The difference is that one holds five coherent blocks and the other holds thirteen separate tiles.

So the concrete opening checklist is short. Discard isolated honours and terminals first. Keep pairs and overlapping tiles in one suit. Prefer wide-open blocks to closed ones. Count the visible copies of the tiles your live blocks need. And judge your hand by whether it holds five blocks, not by whether the tiles look tidy.

It is worth noting what the checklist deliberately leaves out. It says nothing about which suit to favour, because that should follow from where your tiles already cluster rather than from preference. It says nothing about speed versus value, because that choice belongs to the middle game once the hand has a shape. And it says nothing about defence, because in the opening there is no threat to defend against.

Keeping the opening checklist narrow is what makes it usable. A player who tries to optimise everything from turn one ends up paralysed, comparing tile values that will not matter until much later. The opening has one job — establish five live blocks — and doing that well is enough.
After that, the opening is over and the middle game begins — where the question shifts from which tiles to keep to which tiles are safe to throw.

faq.question: What should I discard first in mahjong?
faq.answer: Isolated honour tiles first, then isolated terminals, then middle tiles. This order follows how many future tiles each one can connect with, so you spend early discards on tiles that could never have helped your hand.

faq.question: Are pairs worth keeping in a starting hand?
faq.answer: Usually yes. A pair can develop into a triplet or serve as the pair the finished hand needs, which makes it more flexible than a two-tile sequential block. Keep pairs that have a path and discard ones that do not.

faq.question: What is the strongest two-tile shape to hold?
faq.answer: A two-sided block such as 2-3, which accepts tiles from both ends. Overlapping compound shapes like 2-2-3-3 are stronger still — engine evaluation shows they accept roughly twice as many completing tiles as the equivalent separate blocks.

faq.question: How do I know my opening hand is good?
faq.answer: Count your blocks. A strong opening holds five developable blocks, at least one two-sided shape, and no tile without a path to a set. If several tiles are isolated, the hand is weak regardless of how many suits it covers.

defense-strategy.title: Mahjong Defense: How to Stop Dealing Into Winning Hands
defense-strategy.description: A practical guide to mahjong defence: reading danger, choosing safe tiles, and knowing when to abandon your own hand. Covers suji, visible copies, and the fold decision.

sections.heading: Not Dealing In Is a Skill
body: Most mahjong guides teach you to win. Almost none teach you to lose less, even though the second skill decides more sessions than the first. A player who wins one hand and deals into three has a worse night than a player who wins nothing and pays nothing.

The asymmetry that makes defence worth learning is in the scoring. When you win, you collect from one or sometimes all players, and the amount depends on your hand. When you deal in, you pay a large share — often the full value of a good hand that someone else built patiently. One deal-in can erase two wins.

So defence is not the absence of aggression. It is a separate decision that runs alongside your attacking plan, and it occasionally overrides it. This guide treats it that way: what makes a tile dangerous, how to choose a safe substitute, and when abandoning your hand is the correct play rather than a surrender.

The reason beginners struggle with defence is that it feels like giving up. Building a hand is visibly productive, and discarding safe tiles feels like treading water. But the goal was never to build a hand. It was to finish the session ahead, and sometimes those two goals point in different directions.

There is a measurable way to see the value, which makes the discipline easier to accept. Track a session and count what you paid out versus what you collected. Most beginners find that deal-in payments exceed their winnings even in sessions where they felt they played well. That single comparison is usually enough to convert a reluctant defender into a committed one.

sections.heading: Reading Danger From Discards
body: Every discard on the table is a clue about what its owner does and does not need, and the clues compound into a usable picture of how dangerous each tile is.

Start with suit concentration. A player who discards one suit repeatedly, especially into the late middle game, is not collecting that suit. If their discards are mostly one suit while they never touch another, they are building in the untouched one, and every tile you hold in that suit is a candidate danger.

Next, read call patterns. A player who has called two or three tiles has committed their hand publicly. Their discards from that point are constrained — they are throwing what their finished shape does not need. That constraint is information. A hand still fully concealed tells you much less.

Watch for the tiles a player will not throw. If someone has been discarding freely all game and suddenly starts throwing only tiles already visible on the table, they are playing defence themselves, which tells you their hand is either unfinished or abandoned and they are no longer a threat.

The strongest single signal is a late, deliberate discard. Early discards are noise — a player simply had an unwanted tile. A tile thrown after ten or more turns, when the player has had many chances to use it, says they built around it and did not want it. That says something real about their waiting tiles.

Reading all three opponents at once is beyond most players, and it is not necessary. Identify the one who has committed and is closest to completion. Defend against them specifically and treat the others as background threats.

One further read is worth adding because it is easy and accurate: watch how a player handles their discards physically or in the interface. A player who discards instantly every turn is playing by reflex and their discards carry less information than they appear to. A player who pauses before discarding, especially before throwing a tile that looks harmless, is choosing deliberately — which usually means they are weighing safety, and that they have something to protect.

sections.heading: Suji and the Gap Principle
body: The most useful defensive heuristic in mahjong comes from a structural fact: no two-sided wait can include a tile that sits between two tiles its owner has already discarded.

Here is the reasoning. A two-sided wait needs a block like 2-3, which accepts 1 and 4. For that player to be waiting on that block, they must hold 2 and 3. If they have already discarded the 4, they cannot be holding the 2-3 block, because the 4 would have completed a sequence they had. So a tile discarded by a player makes the tiles that would pair with it in a sequence — the ones two steps away — safer against that player.

This is what players call suji, and the pattern is worth seeing concretely. If a player has discarded 4, then 1 and 7 are safer against them than they look. If they have discarded 1, then 4 is safer. The tiles two steps away from a visible discard lose most of their danger from two-sided waits.

Two limits keep this honest. First, suji only protects against two-sided waits. A player waiting on a closed gap shape or a single tile is not bound by the pattern, and those waits ignore it entirely. Second, respecting suji too rigidly makes you predictable — a strong opponent notices which tiles you treat as safe and works backward to your hand.

Use suji as one input among several. It is a well-founded reason to consider a tile safer. It is not proof, and it never overrides a stronger signal such as a player calling a tile they already discarded.

A useful way to hold suji in your head without memorising tables: for any tile you hold, ask which partial block an opponent would need in order to be waiting on it. If the tiles that would have completed that block are already in their discard pile, the block is impossible and the wait is unlikely. Working backwards from your candidate tile to the shape it would require is faster than learning the pattern as a list of pairs.

sections.heading: Actually Safe: Visible and Dead Tiles
body: Suji tells you a tile is probably safer. There is a category of tile that is genuinely safe, and learning to find them is the core defensive skill.

A tile is safe against a specific opponent if it appears in their own discard pile. They cannot be waiting on a tile they have thrown away — in most rulesets they cannot win on it at all, and in all rulesets they are unlikely to want it. A tile visible in the discards of the player you are worried about is the safest discard available to you.

The next tier is a tile that all four copies of are visible on the table. This is usually called a dead tile. Not only is it unlikely to be wanted, but no player can form a new set with it, so it cannot improve anyone’s hand either.

After those two, the third tier is a tile whose copies are mostly visible. Three visible out of four leaves one copy in play, and the odds any specific player holds it and is waiting on it are low. This tier is not safe in the way the first two are, but it is far better than throwing a fresh middle tile.

The practical procedure, when you must discard and are worried: look at the threatening player’s discards first and take any tile that appears there. If none, look for a fully visible tile. If none, look for a tile with three copies visible. Only when all three tiers are empty do you fall back on judgement and suji.
This procedure is mechanical, which is its virtue. Under time pressure, a beginner’s instinct is to throw whatever looks least useful to them, which is close to the opposite of what defence requires.

There is a fourth tier worth knowing for completeness, though it applies less often. A tile that an opponent has just discarded and that has since been passed over by everyone is unlikely to be a winning tile for anyone, simply because three players had the chance to claim it and none did. This is weaker evidence than a discard pile appearance, but it is a useful tiebreaker when your first three tiers are empty.

sections.heading: When to Abandon Your Hand
body: Defence becomes a real decision only when it costs you something. If your hand is hopeless, folding is free. The hard case is a hand that is close and a threat that is real.

Three conditions together justify folding. Your hand is two or more shanten, so you need more than one lucky draw. The game is late, so few draws remain. And an opponent has shown clear strength by calling tiles and discarding from a narrow range. When all three hold, folding costs little because the hand was unlikely to complete anyway.

The mirror image applies to pushing. Push when your hand is at tenpai, because a single tile finishes you and your wait may land before the threat resolves. Push when your hand has real value, since abandoning it wastes more than the risk of paying.
