Push when the threatening player committed early, which usually means a cheap hand rather than a dangerous one.

There is a middle state that causes the most errors: one tile from ready, with a live threat and several draws left. Here the decision turns on the size of your wait and the size of the threat. A wide wait with three tile types still live is worth defending. A single-tile wait that you can see is half dead is not.

The pattern to internalise is fold early, push late, and never abandon a finished hand out of nerves. Folding a hopeless hand in turn five costs almost nothing. Folding a tenpai hand in the final draws throws away everything you built. Beginners do the reverse, staying in with nothing and then bailing once the hand finally becomes live.

It helps to be precise about what folding costs, because the cost is smaller than it feels. Folding means you stop adding tiles to a hand that was unlikely to finish. You do not forfeit anything you already held, and you keep the option of returning to attack if the threat resolves or a safe opportunity appears. Folding is a pause, not a surrender, and treating it as reversible makes the decision much easier to take.

sections.heading: Defence in Practice
body: Put the mechanics into a sequence you can actually run at the table, because defence fails under time pressure if it requires judgement calls on every tile.
First, track one opponent. The player who has called tiles and is discarding narrowly. Ignore the others until they show similar commitment; splitting attention four ways means you track nobody well.
Second, maintain a mental list of safe tiles against that player. Their discard pile is the list. Any tile you hold that appears there is a free discard you can take whenever you need one.

Third, when you must choose between continuing your hand and discarding safely, ask how far from ready you are. Engine evaluation of your own hand gives a number rather than a feeling, and two or more shanten late in the game is a clear signal to stop building.

Fourth, count visible copies of the tiles you would need. If your remaining path depends on a tile whose copies are mostly gone, the path is not real, and that alone justifies folding regardless of how close the hand looks.

Fifth, accept the result. Defence is measured across many hands, not one. A session where you deal in once instead of four times is a success even if you never win, because the scoring asymmetry means not paying is worth nearly as much as winning.

The satisfying part of defence is that it improves immediately. Attacking well requires reading three opponents and building a hand at the same time. Defending well requires tracking one player and knowing three tiers of safe tile. The second skill is learnable in an afternoon, and it will show up in your results the same week.

faq.question: What is the safest tile to discard in mahjong?
faq.answer: A tile that already appears in the discard pile of the player you are worried about. They cannot win on their own discard. After that, a tile with all four copies visible on the table is the next safest.

faq.question: What is suji in mahjong defense?
faq.answer: Suji uses the fact that two-sided waits cannot contain a tile two steps from a tile the player already discarded. If an opponent has thrown 4, tiles 1 and 7 are safer against them because a 2-3 or 5-6 wait would have used that 4.

faq.question: When should I stop pushing and play defence?
faq.answer: When three conditions hold together: your hand is two or more shanten, the game is late, and an opponent has shown strength by calling tiles. Folding in that spot costs little because the hand was unlikely to finish anyway.

faq.question: Does suji always work?
faq.answer: No. Suji only protects against two-sided waits. A player waiting on a closed gap or a single tile is not bound by the pattern. Treat suji as one reason a tile is safer, not as proof.

common-beginner-mistakes.title: Common Mahjong Mistakes: 10 Errors That Cost You Hands
common-beginner-mistakes.description: The ten mistakes that cost beginner mahjong players the most hands, from calling too often to chasing value, each with the correct play and a concrete example.

sections.heading: Mistakes Are Cheaper to Fix Than to Learn
body: Improving at mahjong is usually taught as accumulating knowledge — more scoring rules, more patterns, more variants. In practice the fastest improvement comes from removing errors, because most beginners lose consistently to the same short list of mistakes rather than to a lack of exotic knowledge.

The reason is compounding. A single wrong early discard costs you a tile of efficiency. The same wrong instinct applied five times in a row costs you the hand. None of the individual decisions looks decisive while it is being made, which is exactly why the errors are so persistent.

This guide collects the ten that do the most damage, ordered roughly by how many hands they cost. Each one gets the mistake, why it seems reasonable while you are making it, and the concrete alternative.

A note on how to use this list. Do not try to fix all ten at once; that produces a player who is thinking about ten things and playing slowly. Pick the one or two that describe your last few games, correct those until they are automatic, then move down the list.

It is also worth saying what this list is not. None of these mistakes are about luck, and none of them are about knowing an obscure rule. They are all about decisions you make on ordinary tiles in ordinary hands, repeatedly. That is precisely why they are worth fixing: the payoff is frequency, not cleverness.

sections.heading: Mistakes 1–3: Calling and Keeping
body: Calling too often is the single most common beginner error. Calling feels productive because it visibly builds your hand, but every call opens your hand, forfeits concealed bonuses in most rulesets, and tells the table what you are collecting. The tile you call must genuinely accelerate the hand, and often it does not — it completes a set you could have finished by drawing while keeping your options open.

Keeping too many pairs is the second. Pairs are good, so beginners keep all of them, and a hand with five pairs has no room for the sequences a completed hand needs. Pairs are worth keeping when they have a path to a triplet or a clear role as the finishing pair. Beyond about two or three, extra pairs are crowding out the blocks that would actually finish the hand.

Keeping isolated honours too long is the third, and it is the mirror image of over-valuing tiles that look important. A lone honour is the most disposable tile in the game — no neighbours, no sequence, needing two specific copies that may be nowhere. Beginners hold them hoping for a triplet and discard useful middle tiles instead. The correct order is honours first, then isolated terminals, then middle tiles.

These three are grouped because they share a root cause: each mistakes visible progress for real progress. A call, a kept pair, a held honour — all three make the hand look more developed than it is. The correction in each case is to ask what the tile or the call is actually contributing, rather than whether it feels like progress.

A concrete illustration of the calling error. You hold a partial hand and someone discards the third tile of a sequence you were building toward. Calling completes that set immediately and feels like a clear gain. But the set you completed was going to finish by drawing anyway within a few turns, and by calling you have opened your hand, forfeited the concealed bonus, and shown the table exactly which suit you are in. You traded a small time saving for a large amount of information and a scoring penalty.

The pair error has a similar shape. Two pairs in a starting hand are good — they give you flexibility and a path to the finishing pair. Five pairs is not five times as good; it is a hand with no sequences and no room to develop one. The moment to stop collecting pairs is the moment you no longer have space for four sets alongside them.

sections.heading: Mistakes 4–6: Value and Speed
body: Chasing a big hand from the start is the fourth mistake. A player decides they want a flush, or an all-triplet hand, and then bends every later decision toward it. The result is a hand that would have completed in a normal shape but never does, because the constraint was imposed before the tiles justified it. Value should be noticed when it arrives, not ordered in advance.

Playing only for speed is the fifth, and it is the opposite error — rarer among beginners but damaging among players who have just learned efficiency. Always building the fastest hand means always collecting the smallest payment and never exploiting the hands where value was genuinely available. Speed is the default, not the only option.

Ignoring the minimum score threshold is the sixth, and it is technical but costly. Several rulesets require a hand to be worth a minimum before it can be declared a win at all. A beginner who completes a hand with no scoring pattern at all discovers, too late, that it cannot be declared. Knowing what your ruleset requires before you start building is not optional information.

The thread through these three is that value and speed are both legitimate, and the error is treating either as a rule rather than a judgement. The player who always chases value and the player who always chases speed are making the same mistake in opposite directions — fixing the decision before seeing the hand.

The minimum score rule deserves one more sentence because it is the only mistake on this list that can make a completed hand worthless. In rulesets with a threshold, a hand that finishes but scores below the minimum cannot be declared at all. That means the hand is not merely low value — it is not a win. Checking the threshold before committing to a shape is therefore not bookkeeping; it is the difference between a hand that counts and one that does not.

sections.heading: Mistakes 7–8: Reading the Table
body: Not watching discards is the seventh and arguably the most expensive on the list. Beginners look at their own hand and the tile just drawn, and treat the rest of the table as decoration. But the discards are the only reliable public information in the game, and a player who never reads them is playing with a fraction of the available data.

The specific failure is most costly in defence. A player who has not been tracking the threatening opponent repeatedly discards into a hand that was visibly nearly complete, then feels unlucky. The information was on the table for several turns; it simply was not read. A minimal version of the habit — track one committed opponent and know which tiles they have discarded — prevents most of these outcomes.

Misreading your own distance to a win is the eighth. Beginners judge closeness by how good the hand looks rather than by how many tiles it needs. A tidy-looking hand with a closed gap wait can be further from completion than a messy-looking one with a two-sided block, because tile efficiency is about how many future tiles you accept, not about how organised the tiles appear in your rack.

The practical substitute for judgement is counting: how many blocks do I hold, how many are complete, and how many tiles would improve each incomplete one. That gives a number rather than an impression, and the number is almost always more accurate than the feeling.

Both mistakes in this pair come from looking inward. The fix in each case is to redirect attention outward — to the table’s discards for the first, and to an objective count for the second. Neither requires new knowledge, only a change in what you are watching.

A quick test tells you which of the two you suffer from more. After your next hand, try to recall the last three tiles each opponent discarded. If you cannot, the discard-reading habit is missing. Then try to state how many tiles your hand needed at the midpoint. If you cannot, the distance-counting habit is missing. Most players fail one of these two cleanly, and that tells them where to start.

sections.heading: Mistakes 9–10: Tempo and Discipline
body: Rushing the turn is the ninth. Under time pressure, players discard the first tile that looks unhelpful rather than comparing their options. Mahjong rewards comparison — the difference between two candidate discards is often measurable, and a player who never pauses will never see it. Slow, deliberate play is not indecision; it is where the skill actually gets applied.

The tenth is the most abstract and the most costly: failing to accept that some hands are not winnable. A player who insists on finishing every hand they start will push past the point where folding was correct, and the accumulated deal-ins will outweigh the occasional extra win. Recognising a dead hand and steering it safely to the end is a skill, not a defeat.
These two are related. Rushing produces shallow decisions; refusing to fold produces bad ones. Both come from treating every hand as though it must be won.

The discipline that fixes both is the same: before deciding, ask what the current hand is actually worth finishing. Some hands deserve aggressive play. Many do not, and identifying which is which is most of what separates a steady player from a volatile one.

It is worth adding a note on how these two feel from the inside, because they are the mistakes most resistant to correction. Rushing feels efficient, and folding feels like losing, so both punish the player who corrects them with an immediate sensation of having done something wrong. The reward for slowing down and for folding properly arrives later and in aggregate, which is why the fix requires trusting the numbers rather than the feeling.

sections.heading: Fixing Them in Order
body: The list is long, so here is the order that pays fastest. Stop calling reflexively. That single change improves both your efficiency and the information you leak, and it takes almost no new knowledge to apply.
Then fix your discard order — honours, then isolated terminals, then middle tiles. This is mechanical and immediately reduces the number of dead tiles you carry into the middle game.
Then start tracking one opponent. Not all three. One player, the one who has shown commitment, and their discard pile. This converts defence from a theory into a habit you can actually run.
Then add the distance check: before discarding, count how many tiles away your hand is. If you cannot answer that roughly, you are choosing blind.

The remaining mistakes — chasing value, ignoring minimum score, insisting on finishing every hand — resolve largely on their own once those four habits are in place, because a player who measures distance and reads the table naturally stops over-committing.

None of these corrections requires memorising a scoring table or learning a new variant. They are changes to what you pay attention to, which is why they show up in results within days rather than months.

One last point about how to judge whether the fixes are working. Do not measure by whether you win more hands; that number is too noisy over a short run to tell you anything. Measure by whether you can describe, for your last few hands, what your distance was and which opponent you were watching. If you can answer those two questions about your own play, the corrections have taken. If you cannot, the mistakes are still running unobserved.

faq.question: What is the most common mahjong mistake?
faq.answer: Calling tiles too often. It feels productive but opens your hand, forfeits concealed bonuses, and tells the table what you are building. Most calls a beginner makes do not meaningfully speed up the hand.

faq.question: Why do I keep losing at mahjong even when my hand looks good?
faq.answer: Usually because the hand is further from completion than it looks. Judge distance by how many tiles your hand still needs and how many tiles each block accepts, not by how tidy the tiles appear.

faq.question: Should I always try to win every hand?
faq.answer: No. Some hands are not winnable, and pushing them leads to deal-ins that cost more than the occasional extra win. Recognising a dead hand and playing it safely is a core skill.

faq.question: What order should I discard tiles in?
faq.answer: Isolated honours first, then isolated terminals, then middle tiles. This follows how many future tiles each can connect with, so early discards go to tiles that could never have completed a set.

discard-strategy.title: Mahjong Discard Strategy: Choosing the Right Tile Every Turn
discard-strategy.description: How to choose what to discard in mahjong: comparing candidate tiles, counting live copies, using the discard pile as a threat map, and handling ties.

sections.heading: One Decision, Every Turn
body: Mahjong hands are won and lost at the discard. You make the decision every single turn, roughly eighteen times per hand, and each one either improves your position or quietly damages it. It is the most repeated decision in the game and therefore the one worth sharpening first.

The decision looks simple — give away one tile you do not need. The difficulty is that you usually have two or three candidates that all look unhelpful, and they are not equivalent. They differ in how much they could help you later, and in how dangerous they are to the other three players.

That is the shape of the problem. A discard is judged on two axes at once: its value to your own hand if kept, and its danger to you if thrown. Most of this guide is about evaluating those two axes separately before combining them.

Beginners tend to judge only the first axis, and often badly. They throw the tile that looks least useful right now, without asking what it could become in three turns or what throwing it tells the table. Both omissions are correctable, and fixing them changes results faster than almost any other adjustment.

There is also a tempo element that makes the discard decision unusual. Unlike most choices in a game, you cannot defer it. You must throw something every turn, and the option of waiting for more information does not exist. That means your discard routine has to work even when you are uncertain, which is why the later sections of this guide spend so much time on defaults and tiebreakers rather than on ideal cases.

sections.heading: Comparing Candidate Discards
body: When you have two or three candidates, the comparison is about what each tile can still become. A tile that can join several different blocks is worth more than one that can join a single specific block, even if both look equally lonely in your rack.

Take a concrete case. You hold 1 and 5 in a suit, and you must discard one. The 1 can only be completed toward 1-2-3, so it needs the 2 and 3 to arrive. The 5 sits in the middle of the suit and can form a sequence with 3-4, 4-6, or 6-7. The 5 is worth substantially more, and if you must choose, the 1 goes first.

The same logic applies to blocks rather than single tiles. Given two partial blocks and the need to cut one, the block that accepts more completing tiles survives. A two-sided block such as 2-3 accepts tiles from both ends. A closed block such as 1-2 accepts from one end only. Where the rest of the hand is equal, keep the two-sided shape.

A worked comparison shows how much this matters. Two hands hold the same nine completed tiles. One has a 2-3 block, the other has a 1-3 gap block. Both look like a partial block of the same size. But the 2-3 accepts two tile types from two directions, while the 1-3 accepts one tile type from the middle. Given a choice, the 2-3 survives every time, and the difference is not subtle — it is roughly double the ways to complete.

Compound shapes deserve special care because they are easy to break by accident. Tiles like 2-2-3-3 look redundant, and a beginner discarding one of them is destroying a shape worth roughly double the equivalent separate blocks. Before discarding from an overlapping run, check whether the overlap is what gives the shape its flexibility.

The exception to all of this is a tile whose completing tiles are visibly gone. Keeping a shape that needs tiles already in the discard pile is not flexibility, it is a dead branch. Count visible copies before you commit to keeping a block.

A second exception is a tile that is far from the rest of your hand in suit. A beautiful two-sided block in a suit where you hold nothing else is worth less than a mediocre block that connects to tiles you already own, because blocks only become sets if they can be joined by the sequences around them. Flexibility measured in isolation is not the same as flexibility in your actual hand.

sections.heading: Counting Live Copies
body: Four copies of every tile exist, and each one you can see reduces what remains. This turns discard choice from an abstract judgement into a countable one.

Suppose your hand’s remaining path runs through tile X, and you can see three of the four copies of X on the table. One copy remains in play, possibly in the wall and possibly in an opponent’s hand. Your path is nearly dead. That is a strong argument to take a different route, even if the route currently looks worse.

The reverse also holds and is more motivating. If none of the copies of the tiles your block needs are visible, that block is at full strength and deserves protection. Holding it is not optimism; it is bookkeeping.

Where this becomes decisive is when comparing two shapes that look equivalent. Both might accept four tile types, but if one set of four is heavily visible and the other is not, the effective value differs sharply. The visible tiles are not just gone for you; their absence tells you the shape is less likely to complete.

The habit to build is narrow. Do not count all thirty-four tile types. Count the specific tiles your one or two live blocks depend on. That is a small enough set to track while the hand develops, and it catches most of the cases where a shape is secretly dead.

There is a useful way to convert this into a decision. When you are choosing between keeping block A and block B, count the visible copies of every tile that would complete each. Whichever block has more live outs is the one to keep, even if it looked weaker before you counted. This is the single most reliable tiebreaker available, and it takes a few seconds.

sections.heading: The Discard Pile as a Threat Map
body: Your discards are a decision. Everyone else’s discards are data. The pile in front of each player is the clearest public information in the game, and it should be running as a background process on every turn.

Three readings matter most. First, concentration: a player discarding one suit while leaving another untouched is building in the untouched suit. Second, timing: an early discard is nearly meaningless, while the same tile thrown after ten turns says the player built around it and did not want it. Third, commitment: a player who has called several tiles has a constrained hand, and their later discards are unusually informative.

The direct use of all this is safety. A tile that appears in the discard pile of the player you are worried about is the safest tile you can throw, because they cannot win on their own discard. That check belongs in your discard routine, before any aesthetic judgement about which tile you would rather lose.

The indirect use is predicting. If a player has discarded 4 and 6 in a suit, the 5 is unlikely to be in their hand, which means your own 5 is safer than its central position suggests. This is the gap principle, and applying it is how a player moves from avoiding obvious mistakes to actively steering.

A practical simplification: track one opponent properly rather than three badly. The one who has called tiles and is discarding narrowly is most likely to win, so their discard pile is the one worth memorising.

The reason the discard pile beats every other information source is that it is authoritative. Body language, timing and hesitation are suggestive but can be faked or misread. A tile on the table is a fact: that player chose not to keep it, and in most rulesets cannot win on it. Building your defensive picture on facts rather than inferences is what makes defence reliable rather than speculative.

sections.heading: When Two Discards Are Equal
body: Often the comparison produces a tie. Two tiles help your hand equally, or the difference is too small to resolve. In that case danger decides, and danger is easier to read than value.

A tile already in the threatening player’s discard pile wins any tie. If neither is there, prefer the tile with more copies visible on the table. If it is still tied, prefer the tile that is further from the middle of its suit — terminals and honours are generally safer than central tiles because fewer waiting shapes need them.

There is a fourth tiebreaker that beginners never consider: the information you leak. Discarding from a suit you have been avoiding tells the table something about your hand. Discarding a tile that keeps your options ambiguous leaks less. When everything else is equal, prefer the discard that reveals least.

This matters more late in the hand. Early on, no opponent can use your discard pattern meaningfully, so the information cost is near zero. In the final few turns, a single revealing discard can tell a strong opponent exactly which tiles you need, and they will hold them.

The order of tiebreakers is worth memorising because it removes hesitation under time pressure: safety against the tracked opponent, then visible copies, then distance from the middle, then information leaked. Applying them in that order costs a second and prevents most rushed errors.

One refinement that matters in the last few turns: when the game is nearly over, information leaked becomes much more valuable to your opponents than it was early on. A single discard that reveals which suit you are waiting on can let a strong opponent hold the exact tile you need and win the race. In the final turns, prefer the discard that says least, even if it is marginally safer to throw a different tile.

sections.heading: A Discard Routine
body: The mechanics above only help if they run every turn without requiring deliberation. So the deliverable of this guide is a routine, short enough to execute reliably at speed.

List your candidates. Usually two or three tiles in your hand are genuinely discardable this turn. Identifying them explicitly prevents the common failure of discarding the first tile that looks wrong.
Compare them on what they could become. A tile that can join more blocks survives. A compound shape is protected. A shape whose completing tiles are mostly visible loses its claim.
Check the tracked opponent’s discard pile. Any candidate appearing there is immediately the best choice, because safety against a committed player outweighs small differences in value.
If the candidates are still tied, apply the tiebreaker order — visible copies, distance from the middle, information leaked.

Then decide, and move on. The point of a routine is speed; a hand played well is not a hand played slowly. The comparison should take a few seconds once the habit forms, and the improvement comes from making the right choice consistently rather than from agonising over individual turns.

The reason this pays off across a session rather than only in dramatic hands is that discards compound. Each correct discard preserves one more option in a hand that needs many. Eighteen small correct decisions per hand do not produce a highlight, but they are how hands that looked unremarkable keep reaching tenpai.

faq.question: How do I decide which tile to discard in mahjong?
faq.answer: Compare your candidates on what each could become, then on danger. Keep the tile that can join more blocks, and prefer to throw tiles already in the discard pile of the opponent you are tracking.

faq.question: Should I discard honours or middle tiles first?
faq.answer: Honours first. A lone honour cannot form a sequence and needs two specific copies, while a middle tile can join blocks from four directions. Discard in order of shrinking options: honours, terminals, then middle tiles.

faq.question: What do other players’ discards tell me?
faq.answer: A tile in an opponent’s discard pile is safe against them, since they cannot win on their own discard. Concentration and timing in their discards also reveal which suit they are collecting and which tiles they no longer need.

faq.question: When two discards are equally useful, what breaks the tie?
faq.answer: Safety first: check the tracked opponent’s discards, then count visible copies, then prefer tiles further from the middle of their suit. Last, prefer the discard that reveals least about your hand.
